If the redness lasts past three days, or your eye hurts, or your vision goes strange, stop and see a cleric. That is not marketing copy. That is the whole instruction manual, and it is sensible.

Mikel Davros, Director of the Potion Evaluation Hall, said the approval "gives consumers a new nonprescription option to manage eye redness conveniently." Convenient it is. I have no quarrel with a tidy little vial for a sore eye. My quarrel is with what I expect to see in the Lower City apothecary windows by Midwinter: banners reading BRIGHT EYES, NO QUESTIONS, priced at a gold piece for a thimble of liquid. I have seen how this goes. A drop that was once a clinic matter becomes a shelf item, and the shelf item becomes a habit.

Here is the plain science, friends. A red eye is a signal, not a stain. Tiny vessels swell because something is bothering the eye: dust, smoke, a late night, a dungeon crawl by torchlight. A drop that tightens those vessels makes the eye look better. It does not fix the dust or the smoke or the three nights you spent reading by a guttering candle. Treat the cause or you will only be treating the mirror.

A recent study of eye strain among scribes found that sleep and screen-free evenings did more for eye comfort than any drop. The old herbals said as much for a thousand years, and I find it rather satisfying when the scholars catch up.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there is already a scrying-glass app that reminds you to blink. Nyx, you have been staring at the glass for nine hours. Go outside. Look at a tree. Let the eyes do the work they were made for.

If your eyes are red tonight, skip the vial and brew a pot of carrot-and-sweet-potato soup, which is good for the eyes and costs about four coppers. Drink it, then go to bed.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

articles.title: 10 Live Birds in His Smalls: Skyport Wardens Cry Fowl
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A traveler allegedly hid 10 live birds in pockets sewn into his underwear at Mirage Bay Skyport. Wardens call it smuggling. Skritch calls it a scoop.
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell past noon, a traveler stepping off an airship from the Nelanther Isles was allegedly stopped at Mirage Bay Skyport with a bulge near his waist and ten live birds hidden in his underwear. The Gatewardens say pockets had been sewn into the garment, and each pocket allegedly held a small plastic tub of bird. A smuggling charge followed.

The traveler, a lawful resident of Waterdeep, allegedly told wardens the birds were "for personal use." Wardens did not ask which personal. He had allegedly written "No" on his customs scroll beside the question about animals, which is technically a statement about the man and not the birds. He was released on a bond of 25,000 gp. The birds, I am told, are fine, and are now in the custody of people with a proper aviary.

I reached the scene by sewer grate, as is my right. "I thought he was just happy to be home," said Tobbin Fenwick, a porter who was eating a pickled egg at the time. "Then something in there went cheep. I put the egg down. I never put the egg down." Fenwick has since finished the egg, allegedly.

The Gatewardens, who answer to the Homeland Watchtower, would not say what kind of birds they were, which is how you know it was a scoop. Rumor at the scanner desk says a customs hound sat down and stared at the man's belt for a full minute, wagging, with the look of a hound who has found the best day of his career.

Look, I have covered the Lower City docks for years and I have seen contraband in barrels, in boots, and once in a very patient cow. Never in the smalls. That takes planning. That takes a needle. Also, somebody at the skyport dropped a silver button near gate nine, and it is gorgeous. Anyway.

The Watchtower reminds all travelers that live birds, like live anything, must be declared on the scroll, and that "personal use" is not a recognized customs category. The Tower District nobles, naturally, say nothing about this, because they smuggle by the crate and call it "imports." Pigeons could not be reached for comment, because I did not look for them.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

articles.title: Mimic Hearing Ends When Witness Chair Eats Exhibit A
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: Chapter 9 ruled a mimic is a monster for hazard pay after the adventuring party's witness chair bit the examiner. The hirelings of the Fourth Attempt win.
articles.content:
BRINDLEMOOR, CHAPTER 9 HEARING ROOM, 0 FEET UNDERGROUND (still checking) — Chapter 9 ruled this morning that a mimic is a monster for the purposes of hazard pay, ending the grievance filed by the hirelings of the Fourth Attempt. The ruling came about four minutes after the witness chair bit the hearing examiner.

The hearing opened on time, which Chapter 9 staff called "unprecedented" and a few called "suspicious." Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor sat at the bench. Ansel Pottage, steward of the hirelings, stood at the lectern with the contract that listed a mimic as furniture, one thumb still in a bandage. The party's bard, who asked to be named, sat in the gallery on what he described as "a very welcoming stool."

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick argued for the guild. Schedule C, he said, covers "miscellaneous furnishings," and a mimic is miscellaneous by nature. Pottage replied that the chest, the stool, and now apparently the witness chair were all in the same room, and asked the examiner to count how many of them had teeth. Oddingwick called this "a leading question about furniture."

The turn came when Brackenmoor asked the mimic, which had been invited and was seated as the witness chair, to state its name for the record. It did not. It closed on her sleeve. She was freed in two minutes by the court usher and a ladle. Her hit points went from 13 to 9, a box score the hearing room's scribe entered in the minutes with visible pleasure.

"The witness has demonstrated its character," Brackenmoor said, rubbing her arm. "Furniture does not do that. A mule might. A mule is a beast and gets hazard pay. I find the mimic is a monster whenever it bites, and I will take no further questions on the stool."

The ruling backdates hazard pay to the first bite and adds one clause: anyone calling a thing "just a chest" must open it first, at their own expense. Pottage called it "fair, and read aloud, which is all I ever ask." Asked about the replacement thumb, he said the guild had "taken it under advisement." Oddingwick said the outcome was a "soft launch of the monster framework" and that Chapter 9 remained "on track."

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society, which had hoped to avoid choosing a claim form, chose the monster form. "It's longer," an adjuster said. "But it has a box for thumbs."

The stool in question has still not been identified as a mimic. It has been taken into Chapter 9's custody and is, for now, being held in the evidence room. The cook who was sitting on it declined to comment. The mimic itself left the building as a bench in the lobby, where it has already bitten two petitioners waiting on permits. Reeve Maudrey Fennick has been asked to rule on whether lobby seating is a monster. She said, "We are aware of the bench."

Ten-foot pole count for the season: eight. The eighth was lost to the lobby bench, which I should have known. I rolled poorly.

— H.D., filing from below

articles.title: Paizo's 13 Omens Horror RPG Launches on Kickstarter
articles.author: Matthias Ashmoor
articles.excerpt: Paizo's rules-lite horror RPG 13 Omens raised $235,084 from 1,702 backers in its first day on Kickstarter. It closes Friday, November 13.
articles.content:
AT THE ASHFORGE — 13 Omens, a rules-lite supernatural horror RPG from Paizo, the publisher of Pathfinder and Starfinder, is live on Kickstarter. The campaign launched October 14 and had raised $235,084 from 1,702 backers by the next morning, ICv2 reports. It closes on Friday, November 13. That is either very good marketing or a very bad sign, and I've hung a horseshoe over the forge door to be safe.

Jason Bulmahn, the lead designer of the original Pathfinder Roleplaying Game, designed it with Joe Pasini, per Tabletop Sentinel, and James Jacobs led narrative development, according to Paizo's blog. The d20 stays home this time; 13 Omens runs on six-siders. Every session is a one-shot with a prologue and three acts that build to a horror-movie climax. One player is the Host, and Paizo recommends four or five others around the table.

The bag of bad luck

The hook is a shared, opaque dice bag. On a check, a player draws two d6s and tries to meet a target number, TTRPG Fans explains. The bag starts with eight Safe dice and one Omen die, and the Host adds more Omen dice from a reserve of 13 as the acts go on. An Omen die that rolls at or below the current act number deals a Wound. The Host never rolls at all. Three Wounds bring a permanent Flaw, and a fourth means death or removal from play. Each character can Cheat Death once per story, or make a Valiant Sacrifice: an automatic success that costs their life.

I reach into a bin of rivets without looking a hundred times a day. Most of what comes out is fine. The far tables are about to find out what happens when it isn't.

The order slip

  • PDF rulebook: $15
  • Physical rulebook: $35
  • Standard physical bundle: $120
  • Top tiers: an online game with one of the designers at $2,500, an in-person game at next year's Gen Con at $5,000, and an "Executive Producer" credit at $10,000, per EN World
  • Dice kit: 21 dice (8 Safe, 13 Omen) and the bag, with a special set made from elk bone (Tabletop Sentinel)
  • Retail release: June 2, 2027 (ICv2)

Paizo will add a retailer tier on October 21 so game stores can preorder the core book, GM screen, and dice, ICv2 reports. EN World says the campaign cleared $150,000 on its first day, and its coverage links a free demo for anyone who wants to shake the bag before pledging. The add-ons also include cards, tokens, plushies, satchels, and skulls, for those who like their dread with merchandise.

— M.A., from the forge

articles.title: Wizards of the Coast Declines to Recognize D&D Union
articles.author: Matthias Ashmoor
articles.excerpt: Wizards of the Coast won't voluntarily recognize the D&D and Studio X union, sending it to an NLRB secret-ballot vote. No date is set yet.
articles.content:
AT THE ASHFORGE — Wizards of the Coast will not voluntarily recognize the union formed by its Dungeons & Dragons team and Studio X, so the question goes to a secret-ballot election run by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). The workers had asked for recognition by October 13. On October 14 the union, United Wizards of the Coast-CWA, posted that the company had declined, and a Wizards spokesperson confirmed it to Wargamer. No vote date has been set.

The whole workforce at the Ashforge is me, the bellows, and an apprentice who mostly sweeps, so I'll leave labor law to the far plane and report what each side has said.

The D&D unit includes D&D Beyond staff, per Dungeons & Dragons Fan. Wargamer describes Studio X as the group that covers most of the creative staff on Magic: The Gathering. Both teams announced on October 6 that they would join United Wizards of the Coast, which is affiliated with the Communication Workers of America. That union formed in June after the MTG Arena development team voted 83% in favor. Wizards did not voluntarily recognize that unit either, Wargamer reports.

What Wizards says

In an internal email to US staff, Wizards' leadership wrote that "we are best able to keep building great games and a great place to work by working directly with employees" and that "Wizards is not neutral on the question of unionization," Dungeons & Dragons Fan reports. The same email said, "in the end, we will respect the results of the election, no matter what our employees choose." It also listed average base salary for individual contributors up 20% since 2023, 2025 bonuses reaching 200% of target, five weeks of paid time off, subsidized medical benefits, and free product.

What the union says

The union is campaigning for fair wages and career progression, job security, remote work protections and sustainable workloads, affordable healthcare, an enforceable AI policy, and ownership of what employees make in their own time, which Wizards currently claims under its IP terms. "We know the workers that make the game can and should be treated better, and our aim is to show that to the world through our union efforts," the D&D team wrote in its October 6 letter, Rascal reported. The organizers say they have "a public supermajority of employees committed to our cause."

What's next

The NLRB will hold a secret-ballot vote of staff in both units. Bell of Lost Souls expects voting as soon as next month; Dungeons & Dragons Fan puts it within several months. Either way, the result will decide whether the people who make D&D and Magic bargain with Wizards as a union.

— M.A., from the forge

articles.title: Starfinder Tech Core Adds Tactical Starship Combat
articles.author: Matthias Ashmoor
articles.excerpt: Paizo's Starfinder Tech Core is out: a 264-page, $69.99 hardcover for Starfinder Second Edition with starship combat and two new classes.
articles.content:
AT THE ASHFORGE — Starfinder Tech Core, the newest rulebook for Paizo's Starfinder Second Edition, went on sale October 7. It's a 264-page hardcover at $69.99, per Paizo's store listing, and its headline feature is tactical starship combat. It also adds two classes, the mechanic and the technomancer. A book whose contents page reads like a parts list has my full attention.

How the ship fights

Starship combat, in chapter 6, runs on two maps at once, lead designer Dustin Knight explained on the Paizo blog. Characters move around a battle map of their own ship and spend their three actions a turn helming a station, repairing damaged areas, bolstering allies, or handling enemies and hazards that turn up aboard. A separate sensor map tracks the distance between ships. There the pilot can Boost Thrusters, Change Heading, or Juke to leave enemy ships open to the gunners.

Each class gets a job. Soldiers fire starship-scale weapons with their own proficiencies and feats and can hit several enemies with Area Fire. Operatives use Aim to deal extra damage to a single ship. Drone pilots plant mines or block incoming attacks, and spellcasters channel spells through the ship's magic conduit. Every battle station has upgrade slots, and Knight's examples include deploying a turret, installing mines into a drone, and turning the ship's prow into a solar weapon for ramming. I once bolted a ram onto a siege cart, but it never ran on a sun. I'm taking notes.

Ships can also take expansion bays such as a medbay or a holoden, plus upgraded escape pods, and the chapter gives guidance for introducing, upgrading, and running starships across a campaign.

The order slip

  • Released: October 7, 2026 (per The Gaming Gang)
  • Price: $69.99 hardcover; Paizo also lists Pocket, Sketch, and Special Editions, and a limited Retailer Edition with a retro game-box cover
  • Pages: 264
  • Classes: mechanic and technomancer
  • Archetypes: nanocyte and junkomancer
  • Ancestries and heritages: robotic SROs, living holograms, and cyborgs
  • Also inside: tech companions, technology feats, armor, weapons, augmentations, magic items, high-tech spells, and sample starship foes and hazards
  • Credits: designed by Jessica Catalan, Dustin Knight, and Aras Yazgan, developed by Jenny Jarzabski and Mike Kimmel, per Angus Abranson's PDF spotlight

The PDF is on DriveThruRPG, Abranson notes. For the record, a junkomancer is the closest thing the far plane has printed to my job description, and I'd like royalties.

— M.A., from the forge

articles.title: Donwald's Sanctions Waiver Spares Damara Oil Tariffs
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A sanctions waiver freed Damara from oil tariffs a day before they started, and Councilors of both parties are furious but in recess.
articles.content:
High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers signed a decree late Friday waiving the sanctions law, the Grimm Damaran Sanctions Act, one day before most of it was due to take effect. The Act placed steep tariffs on any realm buying Damaran oil and fuel. The Senate Chamber passed it 86 to 11, and Donwald signed it himself about a month ago.

Procedure is my religion, so allow me to explain. A sanctions waiver is the part of a law that lets the Seat decline to enforce it "for reasons of national security." The decree gives no end date and gives the reason in one sentence. The reason, as far as the gallery can tell, is a diesel arrangement with Czar Vlad the Bear-Handed. Donwald says the deal will lower fuel prices at home. Earlier this month Donwald also announced an "energy ceasefire" that Vaasa says Damara ignored. Promises Made: two. Promises Kept: a waiver.

The gentleman from the Carolan Reach, Councilor Thornis, a member of Donwald's own Red Oliphant party, called the decree "beyond irresponsible." He asked what part of enforcing a law passed 86 to 11 the Keep fails to understand. I have read the Act. It is eleven pages, and I can report that no part of it is confusing, which is rare for a document produced by this Chamber.

The lady from Mastiffchusetts, Councilor Elizabeth Warrant, said Donwald was "thumbing his nose" at the Council. Grand Vizier Chuck Schemer said the diesel dealings "keep getting dirtier," which is accurate and was, I assume, intended as a pun. Duke Volodar of Vaasa said he hoped the sanctions could be revived. He may be the only person in the matter who has stated a hope and not a position.

Several Councilors have promised a response. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me what that response will be. The Senate Chamber and the Chamber of Commons are both in recess until after the elections. Representative Gregory Meekes of the Chamber of Commons has filed a bill to block the diesel deal. It cannot be voted on until the Chambers reconvene, and by then the fuel will have been delivered and burned.

The waiver is already in force. The Council's two chambers may overturn it only with a vote, and they are not in town to hold one. The motion to recess carried. Nobody objected.

— O.V., from the gallery

articles.title: Midterm Ad Spending Tops 10 Billion Gold Pieces, Loaves Wept
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: Midterm campaign ad spending has passed 10 billion gp, or 166 billion loaves. Barnaby has checked the math. He is not well.
articles.content:
Campaign ad spending for the coming midterm elections has passed 10 billion gp, according to the Ad-Imp Augury Bureau, which tracks every ad the Red Oliphants and Blue Donkeys buy and sells the numbers back to them. The Bureau says the total will keep climbing until Election Day, just under three weeks away.

Ten billion gp is a number I cannot hold in my head, so I held it in loaves. On the Loaf Index, where one honest loaf is 6 copper, that is about 166 billion loaves. (I have checked this four times. I did it again just now. Still 166 billion.) That is a staggering amount of bread, and instead of being eaten it is being spent to tell people a Councilor once voted for something.

The Bureau's figures are specific, so I will be too. The Red Oliphants are outspending the Blue Donkeys by about 11 percent, a gap of roughly 133 million gp. That is 2.2 billion loaves. The Chamber Leadership Hoard, the Oliphants' war chest for Senate Chamber races, is on pace for 310 million gp on its own, or 5.2 billion loaves. Add its six affiliated war chests and the whole network reaches about 643 million gp. I stopped converting at that point because my pencil snapped.

The costliest single contest is in the Lone Star Marches, where about 500 million gp of ads are scheduled, driven by long primaries and a runoff. That is 8.3 billion loaves for one seat. In the Golden Coast, the race for governor is projected at 346 million gp. A Coinlord there spent roughly 210 million gp of his own money on ads and still lost his primary in the summer. I want to be fair to him: 210 million gp is 35 billion loaves, and nobody has ever lost a bread-eating contest that big.

Here is the economics underneath the joke. Ad spending is not coin vanishing into a hole. It lands as revenue for scroll-printers, crier guilds and the scrying-glass networks that carry the ads, which is partly why those businesses love an election year. But the Bureau's count leaves out hundreds of millions in other political spending, and late ad buys are still arriving. The real total will be higher. When something is certain to be larger than the number printed, I tend to lie down.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, received eleven ad scrolls and four crier visits about the Chamber races this week. She says she has never been so well informed and so unable to vote for anyone. She also says the boot is looking better and better. I used to laugh at her.

What this means for your pantry: the ads will end on Election Day, but the flour will not get cheaper. Buy a sack before the next speech.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

articles.title: Bank Earnings: Goldmane Equities Trading Up 72%
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: Bank earnings beat forecasts as Goldmane's equities trading jumps 72%. Sterling Vanmoor calls the 450 million gp charity gift a brand pivot.
articles.content:
The counting houses of the Merchant Princes just posted third-quarter bank earnings, and the numbers are the kind I frame and hang above my sword rack. Goldmane Sacks reported 18.68 billion gp in revenue, with its equities trading desk up 72 percent from last year. Analysts had predicted 17.03 billion gp. They were, if I may say so, thinking too small.

Let me break down the winners. Guildmaster Dravid Solomancer of Goldmane credited the result to clients who "continued to turn to Goldmane for world-class advice, execution and financing." That is thought-leading language. Advisory fees hit a record 1.65 billion gp as merger volume climbed, and I have rarely been prouder of a stack of merging guilds. Assets under supervision reached 4.1 trillion gp. That is a dragon hoard with a compliance department.

Some skeptics will point to the footnotes. The pipeline of future advisory deals shrank. The firm's capital cushion slid from 14.3 to 12.4 percent. And roughly 450 million gp went to its charitable fund, which dented profit. I prefer to call that a brand pivot toward goodwill. Goodwill, for the unfamiliar, is the only asset a guild can print on demand.

Over at Jaypee Morgrim Chasehold, quarterly profit came in at 15.3 billion gp, about 5.57 gp a share. Some bean-counters wanted 5.93. The stock barely moved, which I call a "stability-forward growth posture." Meanwhile Wellspring Fargate took in 21.87 billion gp and its shares slid 3 percent. I'd describe that as "rightsizing the adventuring party's expectations."

I met Guildmaster Solomancer once, at a charity auction in a hall that smelled of old money and mulled wine. He looked at my business card, handed it to a servant, and said, "Keep hustling, young man." I have not stopped hustling since. I have also not been invited back, but that's just the market giving me room to scale. If you want to see how the rest of the Merchant Princes are celebrating, my colleague covered the coin piles hitting record heights, though he seemed gloomy about it. Unions and regulators will always find a cloud around a gold lining. I find the lining.

Goldmane also bought back 2.9 million of its own shares at about 1,049 gp each. A guild that buys itself is a guild that believes in itself. Also, it signed two new acquisitions, because a Q3 without a merger is just a long weekend.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • When your trading desk is up 72 percent, a 450 million gp donation is just a very large networking event.
  • A thinner deal pipeline is only a pipeline that is being gently curated.
  • Always bring a business card, even if it ends up with the servants.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

articles.title: Teachers Strike Vote in Lindenwick: First in 50 Years
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Lindenwick teachers authorized a strike for the first time in nearly 50 years after turning down a 3 percent raise. Brakka did the arithmetic.
articles.content:
Teachers in the Evergreen Reach just held a teachers strike vote and authorized a walkout, the first in nearly fifty years. They will walk out on the 28th unless somebody finds a better offer.

Here is the setup. The Lindenwick Educators' Guild, which speaks for the teachers of the Lindenwick Schoolhouse District, met Tuesday. More than a hundred of them rejected the district's latest offer and voted to strike. They have worked without a contract since term began. Talks started seven months ago. Seven months is long enough to grow a child, and it has not produced a contract.

The offer is a 3 percent raise for the year: 2.6 for the cost of living plus 0.4 for good measure. That means a pay cut with a ribbon on it.

"We are not asking to be rich," said Brindle Oakenshaw, a tutor of arithmetic for fourteen years and one of the Guild's stewards. "We are asking for planning time. A teacher who plans nothing is a teacher improvising in front of thirty children, and some of us have seen how that ends." The Guild also wants more help for the schoolhouse's counselors and mind-healers, and a say in how late-arrival time gets spent. The Guild's president asked for "respect for our time and professional judgment." Fair. That is cheap, and it still hasn't been offered.

The district's superintendent says there is no money. He points to about a million gold pieces lost as enrollment fell, a liability-insurance bill up 84.4 percent in four years, and a 1.1-million-gold-piece hole from the Margrave's underfunding of special schooling. Voters also turned down three bond measures and a levy. "Valuing our employees and protecting the long-term financial health of the district are not opposing responsibilities," he said. Nice sentence. That means no.

The district also notes that teacher pay rose nearly 25 percent over three years and that the average salary last year was 114,711 gold pieces. I have heard that figure before, from guildmasters, usually right before they cut something. An average is how a district buries its worst-paid under its best-paid. Ask the new hire at the bottom of the scale what she earns, then ask what her rent is.

Lindenwick is not a hotbed. The last school walkout nearby was a couple of years back, when the classroom helpers in the next town put down their chalk. Before that you have to go back close to half a century. These are not troublemakers. These are people who color-code their calendars. When they walk out, something has gone badly wrong at the table.

It is the same story Corvallow's town workers told this week: the budget has a hole, the workers are standing next to it, and somehow the hole is their fault. Bargaining resumes Monday at nine in the morning. Bring the money. Bring a lunch break too.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

articles.title: New Tablets Start at 230 gp; Echo Slate Runs on Rival's OS
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Amazoom's new Echo Slate tablets start at 230 gp, run Gargoogle's bazaar, and read your screen. Nyx tested all three. Byte has notes.
articles.content:
Amazoom Caravans has launched a new line of tablets, and I have had all three on my workbench since Wednesday! The Echo Slate 12 Pro, the Echo Slate 11 and the Echo Slate 8 start at 500, 330 and 230 gp, and they went on sale in Waterdeep on the 14th. Every single one is a tablet that finally talks back, and I mean that in the most excited way possible.

First, the big news: these are not another sealed-garden slate. The old Ember tablets are gone, replaced by a clean-sheet design that runs a droid-golem operating system and opens Gargoogle's Bazaar on day one. Amazoom insists this is a brand-new line and not an Ember in a trench coat. I held an Echo Slate next to my last Ember and the trench coat hypothesis is very much alive.

The hardware is gorgeous! The 12 Pro has a 12-inch crystal pane, a 120-beat refresh glyph and a body only six and a half millimeters thick, with an optional anti-glare Nanomatte pane for 550 gp. Amazoom claims nearly triple the mana throughput of the old models and nine times the graphics. I can confirm that my scrying-hockey game now renders the goalie's regret in real time. The 11 comes in Amethyst and Matcha. The 8 weighs 329 grams and comes in aluminum, which is great, because I threw it at a door later and the door lost.

Now the headline feature: Echo Stones Plus lives inside every Slate. Hold the Ask button and the Stone answers from any app. Its On-Screen Intelligence reads whatever is on your display and offers advice, such as picking the best hiking trail from a list of trails. It is off until you opt in, which is a very polite way to say it wants to look at your screen. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, caught a glimpse of the setup menu and said, "Your data is our treasure. Try Echo Plus today."

There is also a new Kindlingscroll reading mode that silences notifications, dims the blue light and promises twenty hours of battery. I read one chapter. A Stone politely suggested a different chapter. Then it suggested a sequel. Then it asked whether I would like to be reminded about the sequel's sequel. The runic latency on that upsell is world-class.

Kid-proof editions of the 8 and 11 ship in padded cases with a year of the Kids' Menagerie subscription, which is the one part I hate. A year of subscription means a second year of subscription, and I will be waiting for that invoice with my eyebrows crossed.

Verdict: Four and a half out of five beholder eyes. The half-eye was deducted because the 12 Pro's optional Pro Keyboard bit me. It was affectionate, probably.

Damage Report: Burns sustained: 1. Doors defeated: 1. Eyebrows: pending. Subscriptions accidentally joined: 2.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

articles.title: Red-Carpet State Visit Leaves Red Oliphants Fuming
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: Senators in the Party of the Red Oliphant blast Donwald's cannon-salute state visit for Emperor Shi, a parley heavy on pageantry and light on results.
articles.content:
Councilors of the Party of the Red Oliphant spent the week angry at their own High Lord over a state visit. High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers rolled out a hundred-foot red carpet, a cannon salute and an honor guard for Celestial Emperor Shi of Kara-Tur. Weeks later, the red carpet is still the only thing anyone can show for it.

I have covered nineteen sieges. This was the first where the host brought the battering ram a bouquet.

The Emperor landed at the Royal Landing Field of Andrewhold. Donwald met him at the foot of the carpet. Handshake: firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected. Which is the problem. The dagger was apparently elsewhere. Councilors learned in a closed-door briefing that Kara-Tur was likely deepening its military ties to Calimshan. They also heard that Calimshan's clerics had used Kara-Tur's eyes-in-the-sky imagery to target Waterdeep's garrisons abroad. Donwald gave the Emperor a tour of the Golden Tower's building projects and a stroll past his Walk of Fame.

Councilor Wicker-Mist, chair of the Chamber's war committee, rose on the floor and said he would have advised against the invitation. Councilor Thornis, retiring and thus free of fear, called the welcome a "what-the-hell moment" and noted the Emperor got a bigger carpet than Duke Volodar of Vaasa ever did. Even the loud scribes of the Oliphant fringe joined in. Rare. Like a dragon agreeing with a knight.

The Golden Tower's reply: the Emperor hosted Donwald in Kara-Tur earlier this year, so the favor was owed. Fair. Armies repay hospitality too, usually with fire.

What did the parley produce? A shared view that the oil strait should stay open, which was already everyone's view. Some trade-ledger chatter. A banquet. No grand bargain on the tariffs, on the arcane engines, on the Eastern Isle, or on the seven-month war with Calimshan that the High Lord is holding off until the ballots are counted. The Blue Donkeys called it pageantry over substance. They are correct, and it costs them nothing to say so.

Tension between the Chamber and the Golden Tower now holds at roughly twelve siege-days. Tension between the Golden Tower and Calimshan holds at about two hundred. Donwald appears to be negotiating with the wrong one of them.

The Emperor went home with his carpet burns and his satellites. Nobody won. Somebody will lose tomorrow, and I suspect it is whoever has troops standing under those satellites.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

articles.title: Sea Ice Hits Record-Low Winter Peak; Frost Giants Evicted
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: Sea ice on the Sea of Moving Ice is thinner and younger, says the Astral Navy, and Brother Wendell prescribes soup for the melting.
articles.content:
Friends, the sea ice is melting again. The Astral Navy reports that winter sea ice on the Sea of Moving Ice tied last year's record-low peak in March, and the September minimum, reached on the twelfth, came in at 1.78 million square miles. That ties three earlier years for the tenth-lowest in about fifty years of scrying-crystal records.

The Navy's polar clerks say what is left is thinner and younger. Old, thick, multiyear ice has declined a great deal, and the thin first-year stuff now does most of the work. I think of it as an infirmary staffed entirely by apprentices. They mean well. They also melt.

Now, the old herbals say nothing about ice, but they do say that a thing cannot be rushed, and a floe that has taken years to thicken does not come back in one cold season. The actual study is the satellite record itself, and it is plain enough. Every summer from 2007 through this one ranks among the twenty lowest on the books. The lowest of all was 2012, which the clerks still discuss the way old soldiers discuss a bad winter campaign.

There is one small mercy. Summer losses have slowed lately, and the clerks say short-term weather can swing the numbers a great deal. I am glad to hear it. I am less glad to hear the fine print, which is that the Sea of Moving Ice could be free of summer ice at least once before the middle of the century. A slow leak is still a leak, friends.

Consider the animals, because I always do. The white bears, the walrus herds, and the seals who raise their pups on that ice have no say in the quarterly reports of any guild. The frost giants who rent the northern floes have already begun filing eviction complaints against the weather. Meanwhile the fire elementals in the great foundries keep chugging along, and nobody asks the seals if they mind. I mind. I mind quite a lot.

The Navy's clerks, to their credit, keep measuring and keep publishing, which is more than can be said for certain potion-makers I will not name. Honest counting is a kind of herbalism. You write down what the plant did, not what you hoped it would do.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil says there is an app that tracks the ice live. Go outside, Nyx, and look at a puddle. For everyone else, this week calls for a pot of hot barley, parsnip, and smoked-trout chowder, thick enough to stand a spoon in, since someone ought to keep things thick.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

articles.title: Copper Thief Dives Through Window, Leaves His ID in Backpack
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A copper thief fled a deputy by diving through a closed window, then left his backpack and driver's license behind. The Watch is allegedly thrilled.
articles.content:
At roughly the third bell after midnight on the first of the month, a deputy of the Oakahoma County Sheriff's Watch was allegedly called to an empty house where a copper thief was allegedly stripping the walls. The thief ran, dove headfirst through a closed window, and vanished. The Watch released the scrying-lens footage this week, and the whole county has watched it eleven times.

The footage is magnificent. The deputy says "Hey!" The thief, mid-pipe, says nothing, because he is already airborne. Glass goes everywhere. Allegedly he did not slow down, and allegedly he did not look back. A bystander named Dolly Quickfinger, who was eating a pickled egg on the porch across the road at the time, said, "I've seen a lot of windows. That one was the fastest window I ever saw lose."

The deputy searched the area with a patrol wagon and a floating observer-eye, both of which found nothing. The thief was gone with his pockets full of copper: wiring, pipe, the innards of an old stove. Not a gold piece in the haul. A hundred coppers make a gold piece, so by my math he risked his face for roughly one decent dinner.

Here is where it gets good. He left his bicycle behind. He left his backpack behind. In the backpack, per the Sheriff's Watch, was his driver's license. Name, face, and home address, all printed neatly on a card he apparently carries to burglaries. The Watch called this "a significant investigative aid." I call it leaving a calling card, and not a fancy one.

He is charged with burglary, resisting arrest, and obstructing an officer, and he has a prior record in the county for theft, drug offenses, and an assault charge. As of the latest reports he is still at large. Allegedly.

Ooh, wait. There is a really nice brass lantern in the evidence photo. Look at the hinges on that thing. Anyway. Sheriff's Watch spokespeople asked anyone with information to come forward, and also asked residents to stop asking whether the window was "okay." Windows, they said, are not witnesses.

Neighbors in the Lower Fields say the old house has been picked clean for a month. "Somebody has to do it, I suppose," said Hobb Tanglebrook, a hay-cart mender. "They just shouldn't use the glass as a door." The Watch agrees on both counts.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

articles.title: Rust Monster Asleep on Level Seven Steps, Guild Sells Tickets
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: Chapter 9 is charging admission to watch a rust monster nap on Level Seven's top step, and the Fourth Attempt has left its armor at home.
articles.content:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 6 — The rust monster that ate the Level Seven ribbon-cutting shears is still asleep on the top step, and Chapter 9 has started charging four silver to look at it. I paid. It is a very large, very round animal, and it snores like a portcullis.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, Chapter 9's spokesman, calls the arrangement "a soft launch of Level Seven." Tickets include a lantern rental, a laminated map, and a waiver against loss of metal. "The level is not open," he told me, "but it is on track, and the monster is part of the track." He then asked me to hold a door. I declined. I always decline.

The trouble is the stairs. Nobody can get past the rust monster without waking it, and nobody can wake it without losing everything iron they own. The Fourth Attempt arrived this morning in boiled leather, a wooden shield, and a sling. Box score: fighter 31 hit points of 38, cleric 22 of 22, wizard 9 of 14, and one hireling holding a spoon carved from a table leg. Their bard, who asked to be named, said the party felt "lighter, and a bit foolish." He did not give his name. Nobody has ever heard it.

The party got within six steps before the monster sneezed. The sling bullets, being lead, were not a problem. The wizard's belt buckle was. He is now holding his trousers up with a ferret, which he says is "temporary."

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the waiver to the end, which is more than the party did. "Clause nine says the guild is not responsible for armor, weapons, buckles, hinges, or 'personal ironwork,'" he said. "I would like it noted that I own a pair of spectacles." He is owed a new pair, he says, and the claim is in.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has refused it. A spokesman said rust monster damage is covered only if the policyholder "did not walk up to the rust monster." Reeve Maudrey Fennick, whose ceremonial chain was among the first casualties, appeared in a replacement made of braided rope and a single brass bell. "We are aware of the monster," she said. "We are aware of the bell." She has asked Chapter 9 to put the ticket money toward a way around the creature, such as a second stair. Oddingwick says a second stair "is on the list."

Ten-foot pole count this season: seven. The seventh went to the monster, which ate it in one bite and looked, I thought, pleased with the effort. I rolled poorly on that one. I held it too close.

Chapter 9 says the level is mostly cleared. The step has a rust monster on it. Mostly is doing a lot of work.

— H.D., filing from below

articles.title: Donwald's Approval Rating Hits Record Low 33% in Realm Poll
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A new poll puts High Lord Donwald's approval rating at a record-low 33 percent, and the Red Oliphants are monitoring the situation, quietly, from far away.
articles.content:
A new poll released Sunday puts High Lord Donwald's approval rating at 33 percent, the lowest figure in the survey's history. The Post-Crier and the Alchemists' Broadcast Chronicle, working with the Ipsissimus Pollsters, asked adults across Waterdeep between the 9th and 13th. Sixty-six percent disapprove. Fifty-two percent disapprove strongly, which the Pollsters describe as "a lot of feelings."

I have sat through four High Lords and have seen approval numbers go down before. This is a record low, down four points since midsummer and eight since last year. The gentleman from the Golden Tower was not available for comment. He was, a courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake informed me, "reviewing the methodology."

The midterm picture is no kinder. Among likely voters, 52 percent would back the Blue Donkey candidate in their district and 44 percent the Red Oliphant, a five-point swing toward the Donkeys since July. A separate scrying of registered voters by a rival chronicle found 55 to 44. Seventy-one percent say the realm is on the wrong road, and 67 percent call the price of lamp oil a serious problem. Both are accurate descriptions of a seven-month war with Calimshan, which the High Council never formally declared and no one has formally ended.

The lady from the Low Country, a Blue Donkey challenger, called the war "a fifty-billion-gold-piece war that is deeply unpopular and misguided," and noted that her fishermen cannot afford the diesel to reach the fish. I record that she is correct on the numbers and has not yet been asked to prove it in committee.

The Red Oliphants are, as the Chamber's pamphlets put it, "monitoring the situation." As I noted when Speaker Johnstone vowed to stay on as leader whatever happened, the party's plan is to remain very calm in the face of each new number. The plan has not yet produced a number worth being calm about.

My running tally stands as follows. Promises Made by the Golden Tower on the war: an uncountable many. Promises Kept: the one that no siege would come before the ballots were counted, which is easy to keep when nobody has scheduled the siege. Election Day is the third of November. The poll is on record. Nobody is reading it.

— O.V., from the gallery

articles.title: Fed Governor Probe: Ivory Keep Names Three-Wizard Tribunal
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: The Ivory Keep's new committee will probe a Fed governor's mortgage paperwork on Nov. 5. Barnaby checked the calendar. Four times.
articles.content:
The Ivory Keep has formed a three-member committee to investigate a Fed governor over alleged false statements on her mortgage application, and its closed-door hearing is set for November 5. (I have checked that date four times.) The governor is Reserve Governor Lysa Kettlebrook of the Federal Reserve of Waterdeep, and she denies everything.

Here is the arithmetic. The Reserve's seven governors set the price of borrowing gold for the whole realm. With the thirty-year home loan already at 7.40 percent, a family borrowing 300,000 gp pays roughly 22,000 gp a year in interest alone, or about 22,000 loaves on the current Loaf Index. Who sits on that bench matters to every pantry in Waterdeep.

The committee will collect evidence, hear from Kettlebrook, accept a written statement, and then report to High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers on whether there is "cause" to remove her. Nobody has charged her with a crime. That is worth repeating, because the memo reads as though somebody already wrote the ending.

You may recall that the High Courts ruled in June that Kettlebrook keeps her seat for now, and that she is owed notice and a chance to respond before anyone removes her. The Keep appears to have read this as a to-do list. Notice: issued. Chance to respond: scheduled for a hearing in the Keep itself, before a panel the Keep appointed. Her scribes say they have "grave doubts" about whether this is a real hearing. I share the doubts, and I have a spreadsheet.

Then there is the date. November 5 falls two days after the midterm elections. The Keep offers no explanation, and I will not guess at one. I will only note that markets dislike surprises almost as much as I dislike the Reserve's recent habit of saying nothing useful, and that Reserve Chair Kevrin Warchest has his hands full with a December rate decision that traders already price as a likely hike.

Why this matters beyond one governor: the Reserve is supposed to be boring. Its power to hold prices steady depends on the realm believing no High Lord can swap its governors when the rates annoy him. If that belief slips, lenders demand more gold to cover the risk, and the extra cost lands on your loan. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, says a boot has never once been investigated. She is not wrong.

I will say the sensible thing, which nobody finds exciting: let the process be a process, let the evidence be evidence, and let both be done in a way the High Courts would recognize. Sound budgets need predictable rulers. Sound loaves need predictable flour.

What this means for your pantry: if you are locking in a home loan, lock it before November 5. Also buy flour.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

articles.title: Antitrust Board Clears 40B GP Merger of Tissues and Tonics
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: Concord regulators approved the merger of a tissue giant and a painkiller maker after forcing a sale of its European hygiene brands. Synergy awaits.
articles.content:
Big news for anyone who has ever sneezed and then had a headache about it. The Sembian Concord's Board of Market Overseers has cleared the roughly 40 billion gp merger of Kimberlee-Cloth Sundries, maker of Kleen-Hex tissues, and Kenvew Apothecaries, maker of Tylenoll Tonic. The antitrust approval came with conditions, and I say that is a feature, not a bug.

Here is the deal in one breath. The Overseers worried that the combined guild would own too much of the shelf in the Concord's realms, specifically the aisle of monthly-comfort goods. So Kimberlee-Cloth agreed to sell every one of its feminine hygiene brands across the Concord, along with the recipes, the trademarks, and the key staff. A food-maker from a distant province will take them over, and an independent trustee will watch the handover. That is not a setback. That is rightsizing the adventuring party before the quest even starts.

Some people see a forced divestiture. I see a clean portfolio. The remaining guild will sell the thing you blow your nose into and the thing you swallow when your head hurts from blowing it. Tell me that is not vertical integration of the common cold. Wipe, dose, repeat. The recurring revenue writes itself.

When I met Guildmaster Jeff Bezoar at a gala last spring, he told me, 'Sterling, every great merger is just two shelves that finally found each other.' He was holding a tissue at the time. I think about that every day. As I covered in the report on the tavern-chain takeover talks, the deal climate is warm. The dating-app buyout earlier this month proved that even the lonely can be acquired.

Skeptics will say a single guild owning both tissue and painkiller leaves commoners with fewer choices at the apothecary. To them I say: choice is a burden. Do you really want to compare forty kinds of soft paper? Let the Overseers do it for you. They already did, and they asked for a divestiture, which is a gentle word for a very large garage sale.

The deal still needs to close, and the Overseers' approval stays conditional on full compliance, so keep your quills ready. But the direction is clear. Bigger guilds, softer landings, fewer sniffles per share.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Every divestiture is a pivot with paperwork.
  • Own the sneeze and the cure, and you own the season.
  • When the regulator asks for a sacrifice, offer the brand you were going to disrupt anyway.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

articles.title: College Strike Averted as 1,500 Lorekeepers Reach Deal
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: A college faculty strike in Chikraggo was called off after a late-night contract deal. Brakka would like to see the actual scroll first.
articles.content:
The college strike is off. Nobody walked out. Nobody lost a day of pay. Somebody in a nice cloak lost a night of sleep, and I'm fine with that.

Around midnight, bargainers for the Cookshire Collegiate Lorekeepers' Guild, Local 1600, shook hands with the Chikraggo Collegiate Halls on a tentative contract. That headed off a strike set for this morning by nearly 1,500 faculty and professional staff. They had voted 96 percent to walk. Tutors, advisers, lab keepers, and lecturers had already been picketing the front steps of the main hall. Then the Halls found their checkbook.

The Guild went in asking for the basics. Better pay. Smaller classes, because forty students per lecturer is a mob, not a seminar. Health coverage a person can actually afford. Free remedial courses, so a student who needs to learn his letters doesn't pay full tuition to do it. And a promise that no thinking-golem will be handed a lecturer's grading quill and a pink slip in the same week.

"I teach rune arithmetic to ninety-one students across four sections," said Mirel Dunmore, a lecturer of nineteen years. "When they said the golem could mark the exams, I asked who would mark the golem. Nobody had an answer. They had a slideshow."

The Halls' statement says the deal "honors the vital work of our educators while ensuring a sustainable future." That means they paid. Probably not all of it. Nobody has seen the scroll yet. The Guild's members get to read it and vote in the coming weeks, which is the part the guildmasters hate and the part that matters.

Across the city, the innkeepers' walkout before the marathon is still going, so Chikraggo is not exactly out of picket signs. Out in Lindenwick, the first teachers' strike authorization in nearly fifty years shows the same pattern. Workers vote overwhelmingly. Management suddenly discovers money. Funny how a deadline does that.

A word to the Guild. Read every line. Check the part about the golems twice. A promise to "explore" something is a promise to do nothing, only slower. And keep the picket signs. You'll want them for the next round of talks.

Meanwhile, Sterling Vanmoor is already on the Yawning Portal circuit calling the deal "a masterclass in stakeholder alignment." It was a masterclass in 96 percent of the membership saying yes to a strike. Learn the lesson properly.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

articles.title: Flying Sports Car Debuts; Teslarc-SpellX Merger Talk Grows
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Muskrat unveils a flying sports car at SpellX's proving grounds, 0-60 in under a second, and the merger rumors finally have a chassis.
articles.content:
Okay. OKAY. Teslarc Carriages has finally unveiled its long-delayed flying sports car, and I watched the whole livestream with my goggles on and my eyebrows already in a protective jar. The prototype, built with SpellX, sits two adventurers, steers by rune instead of wheel, and, when asked nicely, jumps over other carriages and flips in midair on little jets of compressed air. Guildmaster Elon Muskrat called it "something you haven't seen in any play-scrying." He is correct. I have seen a lot of plays.

The numbers! The Rocster, as the broadsheets are calling it, hits 60 miles per hour in under one second. That is the claim on the demo video, anyway. The Guild also says it has the best passive downforce of any road carriage, with wing actuation run off the same firmware glyph that powers its walking tin servants. The runic latency on those wings must be unreal. I would like to feel it. I would like to feel it in a controlled setting, with a cleric nearby.

It comes in three flavors. The Road Edition is open for reservations on the Guild's parchment board. The limited Thrust Edition adds acceleration jets and a multi-mode suction system. The invite-only Rocket Edition actually flies and is not approved for any public road in the realm, which feels like the point. Delivery begins in 2028. The Guild first promised this carriage in 2017, so my familiar Byte, a pseudodragon who speaks only in ad copy, offered the only fair review: "Reserve yours today, and wait with us!"

Now the real show. Every oracle on the Exchange floor heard the same thing under the engines: this is a merger teaser. Muskrat told the crowd the two guilds overlap "on so many fronts," and pointed to Terraforge, their shared rune-chip foundry. One seer called the sports car an engineering showcase with no commercial value beyond embarrassing the old carriage-makers, and added that the Guildmaster simply "can't wait" to fuse his rocket guild with his carriage guild. Teslarc has posted years of falling sales and sells three carriages. SpellX is busy borrowing gold by the dragon-hoard. A flying sports car is a wonderful thing to wave at investors while the paperwork gets sorted.

Markets reacted the way markets do. Teslarc stock rose 0.9 percent, SpellX fell 2.8, and both guilds report earnings this week, one day apart. If you wanted a sign they are already one company, there it is: they spent a whole product launch on a single machine and neither could tell me whose it was. It is also the same Teslarc whose driverless coaches are under inquiry for speeding near schools, which makes the jets feel optimistic.

Do I want one? Desperately. Will it arrive before my current eyebrows grow back, retire, and move to Neverwinter? Unlikely. Four out of five beholder eyes. The fifth is for the delivery date.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below. Burns sustained: 0, but only because it is a livestream. Reservations placed: 1. Eyebrows: pending.

articles.title: Donwald Endorses Nettleyahu Days Before Halruaa Election
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: High Lord Donwald gave Chancellor Nettleyahu a 'complete and total' election endorsement. Halruaa votes in nine days. Voters were not consulted.
articles.content:
High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers has issued a "complete and total endorsement" of Chancellor Nettleyahu the Perennial ahead of the Halruaan election, which is nine days away. The Truthscroll post called the Chancellor a "warrior." Halruaa's voters are the people actually choosing, and nobody asked them first.

I have covered nineteen sieges. This is the first one where the besieging army arrived by endorsement.

The situation on the ground. Nettleyahu is behind in the polls and has been for weeks. His coalition runs on a handful of firebrand allies, chief among them Itamar Ben-Grim, Minister of the Watch. A retired rabbi has now forbidden his followers to vote for Ben-Grim. Nettleyahu, meanwhile, has quietly told envoys of the Sembian Concord that Ben-Grim will not sit in the next government. Ben-Grim has not been told. This is how a flank collapses: politely, and in a whisper.

The opposition is led by Marshal Gadric Eisenknot, a retired war leader with the posture of a man who has seen a real ambush. His answer to the endorsement was short and correct: "Halruaan voters, not Donwald, will choose the next Chancellor." Good line. Plain. No press-release smell on it.

Now the treasury. The Moot is expected to cut every ministry budget by 4.9 percent, about 2.6 billion in Halruaan coin, to pay for urgent weapons orders. The opposition called the cuts "yet another crime by this government." A reasonable man could say both things are true: the cuts are needed, and the timing is a campaign gift nobody asked for.

Handshake assessment, for the record. When Donwald and Nettleyahu meet, the grip is firm, four seconds, with a hand on the shoulder. Two seconds past standard. No hidden dagger detected, but the shoulder pat is a known diversion.

Why does an endorsement from across the sea matter? Because Donwald's favor is a siege engine, and Nettleyahu has been dragging it up the hill for a decade. Rolling it out nine days before the vote tells you the Chancellor's own lines are thin. Meanwhile, back in Waterdeep, the High Lord is also fighting his own midterm campaign. He has time to pick a side in a foreign vote and none to explain why.

Tension on the Halruaan front: roughly sixty siege-days. Nobody has won. Somebody will lose on the twenty-seventh.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

articles.title: Floridia Drought Falls to 25% After Isleias Rains
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: Drought across Floridia fell to a one-year low after Isleias soaked the peninsula, though Brother Wendell says the aquifers are still thirsty.
articles.content:
Friends, some good news for once: the drought in Floridia has shrunk to its smallest size in more than a year. The Realm Drought Ledger reports that the worst-parched ground is gone from the western coast, and Weatherstone, the weather-watching guild, says only 25 percent of the peninsula is still in moderate or severe drought. The rainfall that did it came from Tempest Isleias, which I scolded last week and now must thank, awkwardly.

The details, for those who like their numbers warm. Between the Ledger's two weekly maps, the extreme-drought patches around Tampering Bay vanished and the severe ones shrank to a fraction. A stretch of north-central ground that was in extreme drought a week ago has been marked down to something milder. The Panhandle, bless it, is entirely drought-free. Central Floridia is still abnormally dry, and the far southern swamps remain in moderate drought, which is a funny thing to say about a swamp.

Now, the old herbals say a good soaking rain is worth ten rain-dances, and a study in the Ledger's own reports agrees that a single wet week can lift the map faster than it refills the ground. That is the catch, friends. Surface soil drinks quickly. The deep water under it, the aquifers and wells and old root-cellars, takes much longer to recover. Most of the rain fell in a few days as the storm approached, and the dry season is now arriving right behind it.

Elsewhere the picture is less cheerful. The same Ledger finds that more than half of the lower provinces of Waterdeep, about 53.73 percent, remain in drought, with the lower Great River valley and the southeastern Lone Star Marches getting worse this week. Floridia got a gift. Its neighbors got a shrug.

The Ledger's forecasters add that a warm-current sprite out in the western ocean should hang around through winter, which tends to bring a cooler, wetter season to the south. I would not bet the garden on it. Do the sensible things: mulch your beds, set out a rain barrel, and water the roots, not the leaves. If your well runs low, go easy on the baths until the cellar water comes back up.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there is a scrying app that predicts rain to the minute. Go outside, Nyx. It is damp, it is lovely, and you can feel it on your face for free.

Tonight's recommendation is a thick tomato-and-basil bisque, for a drought that is finally ending and a garden that is surely ready to be eaten.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

articles.title: Dead Tarpon in Truck Bed Lands Angler in Cays Dungeon
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A Mirage Bay angler swore he'd caught nothing, then a deputy found a dead tarpon in his wagon. The catch-and-release law was allegedly very clear.
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell after sundown on Saturday, a marine deputy of the Moonroe County Marine Watch allegedly found a dead tarpon in the bed of a Mirage Bay angler's wagon at Honeyed Bay Preserve, and the angler was jailed overnight on a misdemeanor charge of illegally harvesting the fish. Tarpon are catch-and-release only in the Floridian Cays, which, Skritch is told, is the whole point of tarpon.

The sequence, allegedly, went like this. The deputy strolled up and asked whether the man had caught anything. "Nothing," the angler said. The deputy then looked into the wagon bed, where a large silver fish was lying with the unmistakable calm of the deceased. Nothing, in this case, was about six feet of nothing.

"I was just there for the sunset," said Pim Applewhistle, a halfling who was selling roasted corn from a cart by the parking lot and was eating a cob at the time. "Then I heard 'sir, is that a fish?' and a lot of quiet. Real long quiet. I finished my corn."

The Floridian Fin & Fang Commission is clear on the rules. Any tarpon over forty inches must stay in the water, unless the angler is chasing a realm record and has bought a special tarpon tag, and only one tag is sold per person per year. Nobody has claimed the man had a tag. Nobody has claimed he had a record, either. The Watch says he had a fish, which is a different thing.

Skritch has covered the Lower City docks for years, and he can confirm that fish stories always grow in the telling. This is the first one that shrank to nothing in the telling, then reappeared in a wagon. Also there was a really shiny lure on the evidence table. Very nice. Treble hooks and everything. Anyway.

The man spent the night in the Cays dungeon and is allegedly looking at a misdemeanor, not the gallows. Fishing wardens say the lesson is simple: if the Watch asks whether you caught anything, "no" works best when the wagon agrees. It's not the first odd cargo to turn up in Floridia this season. Skritch's readers will remember the fellow at the Skyport with ten live birds hidden in his breeches, which at least had the decency to be alive.

The tarpon, it should be noted, declined to comment. Allegedly.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

articles.title: Reeve Rules Mimic Lobby Bench a Monster, Orders Sign
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: Reeve Fennick ruled that the mimic posing as Chapter 9's lobby bench is a monster, and ordered a sign. Petitioners now stand; the bench has been fed.
articles.content:
BRINDLEMOOR, CHAPTER 9 LOBBY, 0 FEET UNDERGROUND (the bench disagrees) — Reeve Maudrey Fennick ruled this morning that the mimic posing as Chapter 9's lobby bench is a monster, and ordered the guild to post a sign saying so. The ruling answers the question left open after the hazard pay hearing, in which a mimic seated as the witness chair bit the examiner.

The Reeve took the matter standing up, in the lobby, because nobody in the building would sit. Four petitioners with permit slips had been bitten since Friday. The count by this morning was five. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick argued that a bench is "a fixed amenity" and that the bites were "an unscheduled feature." The Reeve asked him to sit down and make his point from there. He declined.

"Under the ordinance, a mimic that bites is a monster," Fennick said, reading from a page she had clearly written herself, at night, with tea. "The bench bit. The bench is a monster. The bench is also, I am told, load-bearing for the permit queue. Both things are true. We are aware of the bench."

Her order has three parts. Chapter 9 must post a sign reading "THIS SEAT MAY BITE" at knee height, in the common tongue and in Dwarvish. The mimic is to be licensed as a resident monster, which carries a fee Oddingwick estimated at "a modest amount, payable in chairs." And the guild must stop describing the lobby as "fully seated."

Ansel Pottage, steward of the hirelings of the Fourth Attempt, watched from the doorway with his bandaged thumb in his pocket. "I would have asked for the sign in writing," he said. "They have written it. I have read it. It is a good sign." Asked whether the hirelings would seek further pay for the bench, he said the contract was "still being read, slowly, in case it bites."

Chapter 9 responded within the hour by announcing a cushion programme. Petitioners may now rent a folding stool for two silver, "a neutral surface," Oddingwick said. The stool is not, at press time, a mimic. I checked it with the pole. Ten-foot pole count for the season: nine. The ninth was the bench's, and I should have seen that coming. I rolled poorly.

The mimic itself had no comment, being a bench. The party's bard, who asked to be named, did offer one after sitting on a rented stool for eleven minutes. "It has a very welcoming look," he said, and stood up quite fast.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society said claims for lobby bites will go on the monster form, now with a box for thumbs and a new box for "furniture, formerly." The unidentified stool remains in the evidence room. Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor, who was bitten at the hearing and has not forgiven the ladle's absence, is reported to have walked past the lobby twice this morning without looking left. The Reeve will rule next on the evidence room.

— H.D., filing from below

articles.title: Existing-Home Sales Hit 3.99M as Hearth Prices Climb
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: Existing-home sales rose 1.5% to 3.99 million, yet the median home price climbed for a 39th straight month. Barnaby counts the loaves and sits down.
articles.content:
Existing-home sales across Waterdeep rose 1.5% in September to a yearly pace of 3.99 million, the National Guild of Realm-Tors reported Friday. That sounds like good news until you notice that the median home price also rose, to 417,500 gold pieces, which is the 39th month in a row it has gone up. (I have checked this four times. It is still 39.)

On the Loaf Index, at four gold pieces a loaf, the typical hearth-and-roof now costs 104,375 loaves. That is a great many loaves. A baker working without sleep, stopping only to weep into the dough, could not produce them before the next Harvest Moon.

Here is the economics underneath. Sales rose a little from August, but they are still 2.2% below last year. Fewer buyers qualify because borrowing got dearer: the weekly hearth-loan rate keeps climbing, and Fraddie Mace Home-Loan Hall says the average 30-year loan cost 6.86% in September, up from 6.35% a year ago. On a loan of 334,000 gp, that extra half point is about 1,700 gp a year, or 425 loaves. Every year. Forever. (I did this one five times.)

Laurence Yawn, Chief Counter of the Realm-Tors, put it plainly: "Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home." I agree with Master Yawn, which is rare for me and a little frightening.

There is one thing for a nervous halfling to cling to. Unsold hearths number 1.60 million, a 4.8-month supply, and the typical listing now sits 33 days instead of 31. Sellers are, for the first time in ages, being made to wait. Sterling Vanmoor says this is a "buyer's window of opportunity." Sterling Vanmoor has never once paid a hearth-loan, and would not know a window from a drawbridge.

The sensible reading is dull: prices are sticky because owners with cheap old loans will not sell and take a dearer one, so supply stays thin even when it looks plump. Houses are not getting cheaper; buyers are just getting fewer. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, says a boot has never had a variable rate. I used to laugh at her.

What this means for your pantry: if you are buying a hearth, do the arithmetic on the loan, not the price, and keep six months of flour in reserve. If you are renting, buy flour anyway.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Hearth-Deed Waiting Game
hook.text: A young couple needs a deed sealed before the guild's loan rate lock expires in three days, but the seller has vanished. Someone is quietly buying up empty hearths and sitting on them to keep the price rising.

npc.name: Odo Pennyfeather
npc.want: To close one honest sale before the quarter ends and his ledger shames him.
npc.secret: He has been backdating listings for a landlord who owns half the lane.

location.name: The Vacant Row
location.text: A lane of twelve tidy cottages with lit windows and no residents, all sold in one season. The chimneys smoke on a schedule, as if someone is paying to make them look lived in.

campaign.rumor: They say the empty cottages on the Vacant Row are owned by a single dragon who finds rent more agreeable than hoarding.

articles.title: Grad Student Strike Set for Oct. 27 at Harrowmoor
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Over 4,000 apprentice scholars will strike again on Oct. 27 unless Harrowmoor pays up. The grad student strike follows a 40-day walkout last spring.
articles.content:
The apprentices are walking out again. The grad student strike is on for the 27th.

The Apprentice Scholars' Lodge at Harrowmoor Arcane University, a branch of the United Axlewrights, says its 4,000-plus members will strike on the 27th unless a contract lands first. It would be the second grad student strike this year. The first ran forty days last spring. In an early-month vote, 88 percent of the Lodge backed going out again.

Here is what the Lodge asked for: raises, protection for scholars from foreign realms, and a grievance hearing run by someone who does not draw a Harrowmoor salary. Here is what Harrowmoor gave. After the session on the 8th, the Provost's office raised its yearly raise from two and a half and two and three-quarters percent to three. The Lodge called it the first new offer in three sessions. Three sessions. I have seen mine foremen move faster, and mine foremen are stone.

The university also wants to scrap nearly three million in gold that helps scholars pay for healing, teeth, child-minding and immigration scrolls. Harrowmoor will not drop that one. Its endowment, meanwhile, swelled to almost sixty-eight billion this year.

Harrowmoor says it has offered a 6.1 percent raise the moment a contract is signed and nearly sixteen percent over its life. Its spokesman says a strike is 'not warranted.' That means: please go back to grading.

Then came the letter. On the 2nd, the Provost's office warned the faculty that a second strike might count as 'intermittent,' and that striking scholars could face 'employment consequences.' That means they might fire them.

'I teach three sections of Elementary Alchemy and grade two hundred scrolls a week,' said Odrin Vellacott, a fourth-year apprentice and part-time potion-lab proctor. 'They say my job is a stepping stone. I have been standing on this stone for six years and it has not moved.'

The Lodge says it will not be scared off by what its vice-steward called 'unlawful attempts to stop workers from engaging in collective action.' It has asked for more bargaining dates before the deadline. Harrowmoor has not said yes.

Nobody wants a strike. A strike means no lunch, cold feet and a picket line in October wind. But a school that can find sixty-eight billion for its vault can find three million for a child-minder's wage. Pay the apprentices. Then eat your lunch, everyone.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Apprentices' Picket
hook.text: The scribes' college is days from a walkout, and the provost has quietly hired sellswords to guard the grading hall. Strikers want the party to carry a sealed grievance scroll past the guards to an independent magistrate before the deadline.

npc.name: Odrin Vellacott
npc.want: A signed contract before the deadline so nobody loses their stipend.
npc.secret: He has already received a private offer of a lecturer post if he talks the strikers down.

location.name: The Cold Ladle Kitchen
location.text: A soup hall run out of a disused chapel where strikers share meals between shifts on the line. The cellar holds the strike fund, and someone has been counting it twice.

campaign.rumor: They say the provost's office has a list of every striker's name and where they sleep, and that it is longer than the contract.

articles.title: Protests Draw 9,000 Guards as Probowl Hits Two Years
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: Indonessar stations 9,000 guards ahead of protests marking two years of High Lord Probowl, who calls the show of force 'hospitality'.
articles.content:
Indonessar will put more than 9,000 guards on the streets of its capital today as protests mark two years of High Lord Probowl Subiantor in power. That is the number. Nine thousand. Count them twice.

The target is the Marble Square outside the Assembly. The Indonessar Isles are an archipelago, which means a capital is a long way from most of its people, and today those people are coming anyway. Lamp-oil prices climbed again this autumn. Last year's riots over councilor perks ended with thousands in the stockades. Nobody has forgotten, including the guards.

I watched the briefing. Probowl's spokesman called the deployment "a gesture of hospitality." Hospitality. Nine thousand hosts, shields polished, no refreshments. I have been to sieges with warmer hospitality and fewer hosts.

Probowl is a former warlord. He understands crowds the way a quartermaster understands grain: how much, where stored, when it spoils. His approval is down in the high thirties. He walked onto the parapet this morning and waved. Wave: brief, open palm, no hidden dagger detected. The crowd waved back with fewer fingers.

Tension in the capital stands at roughly twelve siege-days, climbing. Marble Square holds perhaps fifty thousand. The guards are outnumbered, and the guards know it, which is why there are nine thousand of them and not nine hundred. Arithmetic is the only honest enemy in this war.

I will say this for the Watch commanders: they published their numbers in advance. That is more than any press release has ever done. I hate press releases. I respect a plain count of spears.

Ottoline Vex will file from a gallery seat with a view of the Assembly's fountain and call it "a tense morning." From the street, it is a tense afternoon, a tense evening, and a long walk to the nearest ration cart. The rations here are fried rice with an egg on top. I have eaten four plates. Best thing in the dispatch.

The lesson of every protest is the same. The crowd wants lower prices and a hearing. The leader wants the crowd home before the supper bells. Nine thousand guards means he does not expect a hearing. Watch the side streets at dusk. That is where the parley is decided.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: Nine Thousand Spears
hook.text: A strongman's guard is massing around the city square before a protest, and the party's friend among the demonstrators has gone missing with a ledger of stolen lamp-oil taxes. The party must find the ledger before either side turns the square into a battlefield.

npc.name: Sitorra Wibowe
npc.want: To march a peaceful crowd to the Assembly and be heard.
npc.secret: She is secretly paying two guards to warn her which streets will be sealed.

location.name: Marble Square
location.text: A vast paved plaza before the Assembly, ringed by shuttered stalls. Every fountain has been drained, supposedly for maintenance.

campaign.rumor: They say half the guards on the square are being paid in lamp oil, and none of them want to hold the line.

articles.title: Young Red Dragon Seeks Permit to Extend Hoard Under Tavern Row
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: A young red dragon asked the Cellars Board to extend its hoard under three Tanner's Row cellars. The Sleeping Mule's is one of them.
articles.content:
BRINDLEMOOR CELLARS BOARD, HEARING ROOM B, ZERO FEET UNDERGROUND (A RELIEF) — A young red dragon named Skorvath applied Tuesday for a permit to extend its hoard beneath three cellars on Tanner's Row. The Brindlemoor Public Cellars Board heard the petition for four hours and decided nothing, which Chapter 9 called "on track."

Skorvath, who attended in the form the Board's clerk described as "mostly door-sized," says its current hoard of 11,400 gold pieces has outgrown its lair under the old tannery. The proposed extension would run under the Sleeping Mule, the Candlewick pawnshop and a chandler's. Skorvath offered to pay rent, in coin, from the hoard itself. Several board members noted this is the first time a tenant has offered to pay the landlord with the landlord's own floor.

"We have excavated before," said Inspector Corwin Tallowby, who read out the application. "We have never excavated toward a dragon." Tallowby, last seen citing the Mule for an unlicensed gelatinous cube in the walk-in, said the dragon's paperwork was the tidiest he had received this season. He then said he was not complimenting it.

The dragon's counsel, a tired kobold named Pip, argued that a hoard is "a storage use, not a residential one," and that Skorvath only sleeps on it. Opposing counsel, a chandler named Hilde Vantrop, argued that the same is true of her shop's candles, and nobody has ever asked her to burn the neighborhood. Skorvath asked that the record show it has burned the neighborhood twice, "both accidents, both small."

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, the one party whose cellar is directly affected, did not object. "It's a deep cellar. It's got a draft. A dragon takes the chill off the cider," she said. Harrowgate has extended credit to a cube, a ghost and a man who claimed to be a ghost. She says a dragon with a hoard is the best credit risk she has met.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick, who attended in a fire-resistant chain, said only: "We are aware of the dragon." She asked the Board to consider whether a cast of Stone Shape could be used to build the extension without disturbing the foundations. A Board mason said it could, and added that the foundations were already disturbed, by the cube, and before that by something nobody wrote down.

Hit points, for those keeping a box score: Skorvath, 178 of 178. Inspector Tallowby, 22 of 22, though he sat very still. The party's bard, who asked to be named, was present and says the dragon "has a good speaking voice," and that he is prepared to write a ballad if the permit passes and a different ballad if it does not. This is my seventh ten-foot pole of the season, which I lost testing the hearing room floor. It was not a mimic. I rolled poorly on whether it would be.
