location.text: A landing at the bottom of an unmapped stairwell, scattered with chewed nail heads and one sleeping rust monster. The walls are bare of metal fittings; every hinge was eaten years ago.

campaign.rumor: They say the nails were never meant to lead the monster away, only to lead something else up.

articles.title: Alarm Spell Wakes Party 14 Times During One Long Rest
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: The Mudsock Vanguard cast Alarm around camp for a safe long rest. Squirrels, a moth, and their own rogue woke them 14 times. Nyx loved it. Byte did not.
articles.social: The Mudsock Vanguard cast Alarm around their camp for one safe long rest. It went off 14 times: nine squirrels, one moth, and their own rogue going to pee four times. The wizard now has zero spell slots back. Would you have kept the alarm, or dispelled it at 2 a.m.?
articles.content:
Brindlemoor's Mudsock Vanguard cast the Alarm spell around their camp on the Undermaw's second landing this week, hoping for one uninterrupted long rest. They got fourteen interruptions instead. I have been reviewing the ward ever since, because I am a professional and also because I couldn't sleep either!

Here is the log, as read back by the party's wizard, Pennick Thrallowby. The first four alerts were squirrels. The fifth was a moth. Pennick says it was "a very small moth," and Alarm, which has no concept of small, rang the mental chime at full volume. Alerts six through nine were more squirrels, possibly the same squirrel, who appears to have started charging the perimeter for sport. Alerts ten, eleven, twelve and fourteen were the party's own rogue, Dessa Quillfoot, walking out of the ward to pee and walking back in.

"I whispered that I was going out," Dessa said. "The ward doesn't care that I whispered. It cares that I crossed it. Four times. Nobody warned me about the bladder tax."

The runic latency is outstanding. Alert thirteen, which was a genuine owlbear-sized shape at the edge of the clearing, arrived in under a second, and I would like that on the box. It turned out to be a cart. The cart was empty. Nobody could tell me why a cart was in a clearing in the Undermaw, and nobody had the strength to ask.

The core problem is mana throughput. Alarm sounds in the caster's head only, so Pennick took every alert alone while the rest of the party snored. By dawn the cleric had her prayers back, the fighter had his hit dice, and the wizard had a twitch. A long rest needs eight hours with no more than two of strenuous activity, and the Guild's own pamphlet says so. Chapter 9 declined to comment on whether a rogue's bathroom schedule counts as strenuous.

My familiar Byte, who sat through the entire demo, said "Alarm. Because you deserve to wake up." He then bit the moth. I assume that is a ruling.

Pennick has since switched to a different method, which is sleeping in shifts and trusting the dog. He also asked me to note that he is "not mad, just thin." Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to touch grass, but the grass is where the squirrels live, Wendell.

Four out of five beholder eyes. The ward works exactly as written, and that is the whole problem.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Alerts sustained: 14. Squirrels: 9 (or 1). Moths bitten: 1. Spell slots recovered: 0. Eyebrows: fine, but I am very tired.

hook.title: Fourteen Alerts Till Dawn
hook.text: A warded camp keeps setting off for the smallest things, but alert thirteen was a real intruder: someone left an empty cart in the clearing so the party would stay up. A caravan master nearby wants to know who is scouting her route and will pay for answers.

npc.name: Pennick Thrallowby
npc.want: One full night of sleep, at any price.
npc.secret: He cast Alarm twice by mistake, which is why the moth rang so loud.

location.name: The Second Landing Camp
location.text: A cleared ledge on the Undermaw's second level with a ring of scorched stones and a well-trodden path of squirrel tracks. The empty cart sits at the edge, and its wheels have fresh grease.

campaign.rumor: They say the squirrels down there are paid by the night and that the moth was a spy.

articles.title: Adventuring Party Votes Six Hours on Two Dungeon Doors
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party on Level Three of the Undermaw spent six hours voting on which of two doors to open, and finished in the dark.
articles.social: A five-member adventuring party in the Undermaw spent six hours on a formal vote over two doors. There were three amendments and one recount, and all six torches burned out first. A skeleton waited the whole time. Which door would you have opened?
articles.content:
An adventuring party called the Copper Candle Company spent six hours on Level Three of the Undermaw on Saturday voting on which of two dungeon doors to open. By the time they reached a result, all six of their torches had burned out, which the minutes record as 'a matter for the next session.'

The trouble began when Dunstan Mirelle, a dwarf cleric, rose to move that the party 'consider the door on the left.' The gentleman from the rear guard, a halfling archer, seconded it and immediately offered an amendment to consider the door on the right instead. A point of order followed on whether an amendment may undo the motion it amends. The party's wizard held that it may. The party's fighter held that she was hungry.

The first vote split two to two, with the rogue abstaining on the grounds that doors were 'a conflict of interest.' She has picked locks professionally for eleven years. A recount was requested and granted. It also came out two to two, though the minutes note that one member voted twice in a spirit of enthusiasm.

Three amendments then reached the floor. One proposed opening the left door but with a rope. One proposed opening neither and having a snack. The third, from the wizard, proposed forming a subcommittee of one to examine the doors, which would have been the wizard. It was ruled out of order by the chair, who was also the wizard's brother-in-law.

By my count the party made nine procedural promises during the evening, including 'we will be brief,' and kept the one about adjourning, though not on time. The torch situation was raised at hour three. A motion to light a seventh torch failed because the party had packed six. The motion carried, in the sense that nobody opposed it, but it did not produce a torch. Nobody read it.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the doors were 'the least interesting thing in that corridor.' He was right. At the sixth hour, a wandering skeleton from behind the left door knocked politely and asked whether the party intended to use the passage, as it had been waiting since supper. The party moved to table the question. The skeleton seconded.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the guild 'has every confidence in the party's process' and that delve permits do not specify how doors are chosen. 'We are aware of the voting,' he said. 'It is on track.' Reeve Fennick declined comment, having recently sat through thirteen days of a ghost.

The Copper Candle Company has scheduled a follow-up session for Saturday. The agenda lists one item: the door on the right, subject to amendment.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Door by Committee
hook.text: A rival party has gotten stuck in a corridor, arguing over two doors, and has been there so long that something patient is queuing behind one of them. A worried hireling pays the party to break the deadlock before the torches go out.

npc.name: Perrin Quill
npc.want: To get the minutes signed and everyone out of the corridor alive.
npc.secret: Perrin has been quietly rewriting the votes so the party never reaches a decision, because both doors scare them.

location.name: The Corridor of Two Doors
location.text: A narrow passage on a dungeon level with an identical door at each end, one scratched with a left-hand mark and one with a right. The air is stale, and a faint line of chalk tally marks runs along the wall.

campaign.rumor: They say the skeleton behind the left door has been waiting so long that it has started paying rent.

articles.title: Owlbear Naps in Laundry Cart; Fish Street Waits 2 Days
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: An owlbear fell asleep in a laundry cart on Fish Street and has not moved in two days. The Constabulary says nobody is waking it. Allegedly.
articles.social: An owlbear has been asleep in a laundry cart on Fish Street for two days. The Constabulary has put up 14 rope posts and a sign reading 'Please Do Not.' Laundress Pim Oddlow says 61 households are missing their sheets. Would you be the one to wake it?
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell after midnight on Sunday, an owlbear climbed into a laundry cart on Fish Street, curled up on 61 households' worth of clean sheets, and went to sleep. Two days later it is still there, and the Constabulary has declined to wake it. Allegedly this is policy.

'We are monitoring the situation,' said Constabulary Sergeant Brom Teasel, who was monitoring it from the far side of a pie stall. 'It snores. The snore has a beak in it. We have put up 14 rope posts and a sign that says Please Do Not.' The sign was allegedly chewed by lunchtime. The rope posts are fine. The posts are not the problem.

The sheets belong to Pim Oddlow, a laundress, who says the cart held every bedsheet on the east side of the street, freshly pressed. 'Sixty-one households,' she said, wringing a towel at the time. 'Sixty-one beds with nothing on them. The owlbear has not paid for the starch.' Oddlow estimates the loss at 38 gold, plus whatever the owlbear is doing to the pillowcases, which she described only as 'nesting.'

Neighbors have organized. Corvin Stubb, a baker, was holding a tray of rolls when he told me the street is 'quiet for the first time in years,' and that business is up because gawkers buy snacks. A rival baker on the other side of the road reported the opposite. A third man, who gave his name only as Dobbin and was eating a turkey leg, said he is fine with the owlbear but wants it known that he saw the cart first. Nobody asked him.

Also there is a really nice brass lantern hook two doors down, just sitting there, very shiny. Anyway. Recovered.

The Tower District has weighed in. A nobles' committee, speaking from a safe distance of eleven miles, called the situation 'a failure of Lower City sanitation' and asked that the owlbear be moved somewhere less visible. Fish Street's answer was to hang the committee's letter on the rope posts as decoration. Skritch is told the owlbear has not read it. Skritch is also told that pigeons have started roosting on its back, which is the single worst development of the week.

Sergeant Teasel says the Constabulary will act when the owlbear wakes on its own, or when the sheets need to be returned, whichever comes later. He has asked the public not to throw anything at it, not to sing to it, and not to try to borrow a pillowcase. Three people have reportedly tried to borrow a pillowcase. One of them is Dobbin.

For now, Fish Street runs on tiptoe, and the laundry cart rolls nowhere. The Constabulary says the matter is under control. Allegedly.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Sleeper in the Cart
hook.text: An owlbear has bedded down in a laundress's cart full of the town's sheets, and the guard won't touch it. The laundress will pay 40 gp to anyone who gets the sheets back without waking it.

npc.name: Pim Oddlow
npc.want: Recover every sheet before customers demand refunds.
npc.secret: She has been quietly feeding the owlbear sausages so it won't wake up.

location.name: Oddlow's Wash and Press
location.text: A steamy laundry on a crowded street, with sheets strung across the alley like sails. The back room has a trapdoor the owlbear has not noticed yet.

campaign.rumor: They say the owlbear isn't sleeping at all, it's brooding, and those pillowcases are eggs.

articles.title: Adventuring Party Haggles an Hour, Pays 8 gp Over Sticker
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party haggled an hour over 3 silver on a potion of healing and paid 58 gp, 7 sp against a 50 gp sticker. Sterling Vanmoor is inspired.
articles.social: A Brindlemoor adventuring party haggled an hour over 3 silver on a 50 gp potion of healing. They paid 58 gp, 7 sp, after fees for candle, chair and the mule. The shopkeeper called it a fair deal. Would you have just paid the sticker?
articles.content:
An adventuring party called the Salt Road Six spent a full hour haggling over 3 silver on a single potion of healing in Brindlemoor on Saturday, and walked out paying 58 gp, 7 sp against a posted price of 50 gp. The shop is Halsk's Curios and Cordials on Tanner's Row. Its owner, Dorrin Halsk, calls the result "a deal both sides can feel something about."

Some people see eight and a half extra gold pieces. I see the best-executed customer journey of the quarter. The Salt Road Six came in with a plan, a rogue who "reads people," and a bard who offered to pay in exposure. Halsk opened with a firm 50 gp. The party countered at 49 gp, 7 sp. Forty minutes of eye contact followed.

Here is where the pivot happened. Halsk, a true thought-leader in retail, introduced a negotiation consultation fee of 1 gp per quarter hour, billed to whoever spoke first. Then came the candle surcharge (2 gp, because haggling "burns light"), the chair fee (3 sp each, six chairs), and mule parking at 4 gp, which the party's mule had not asked for and could not refuse. By the time the rogue said "fine, fifty," the sticker price was a fond memory.

"We saved three silver on the potion," said the party's rogue, Hesper Moult, holding her receipt. "It says so right here, under the line that says 'Rogue's Discount Applied, Then Reversed.'" Her bard, asked whether the hour was worth it, said the experience had been "a journey."

Shieldwall Mutual has declined to comment, though a clerk confirmed the policy excludes any loss the party was warned about, including the chair fee. The Salt Road Six plan to haggle again next week, this time at a rival shop. Halsk says he will welcome them with open arms and a fresh price list.

I met a retired guildmaster of the Copper Exchange at a gala once, and he told me, "Sterling, the customer who haggles has already agreed to pay. All that's left is the amount." I think about that every day. I also think about it whenever I see a mule.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Never haggle in a chair you haven't priced.
  • If the shopkeeper smiles, you are already the product.
  • A discount that is later reversed is just a loyalty program.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Chair Fee Racket
hook.text: A shopkeeper has been bleeding parties dry with invented surcharges, and a furious guild clerk wants proof before the town magistrate will act. The party must haggle in the shop and keep every receipt.

npc.name: Dorrin Halsk
npc.want: To keep every haggler paying for the privilege of haggling.
npc.secret: He has been splitting the surcharges with the mule stable next door.

location.name: Halsk's Curios and Cordials
location.text: A narrow shop with a price list that grows longer each visit. The six chairs are bolted to the floor and each has a tiny brass meter.

campaign.rumor: They say the shopkeeper's candle surcharge pays for a second candle that nobody has ever seen lit.

articles.title: Sleep Spell Drops 57 Brindlemoor Folk in the Extra Hour
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: A sleep spell cast to save the extra hour when Brindlemoor set its clocks back put 57 folk to sleep on their feet. Brother Wendell prescribes soup.
articles.social: When Brindlemoor set its clocks back Sunday, an apprentice cast a sleep spell to bank the extra hour. It dropped 57 folk, one of them mid-sermon. The Sleeping Mule had to stack three of them like firewood. Would you spend the extra hour asleep, or awake?
articles.content:
Friends, a sleep spell cast to save the extra hour on the night Brindlemoor set its clocks back has put 57 townsfolk to sleep where they stood. The apprentice responsible, a lad named Ferrin Quill, told the Reeve's office he "only wanted a little extra rest for the town." The spell, as spells do, took it literally.

The clocks fell back at the second bell on Sunday morning, as they do every autumn, and Brindlemoor gained one hour it had not planned for. By the old herbals, an extra hour is a gift from the Harvest Mother. By Chapter 9, it is "an unlicensed hour," and the town's bell tower is still being scraped, so nobody was in a mood to argue.

Apprentice Quill reportedly cast sleep from the steps of the Sleeping Mule at about the stroke of the repeated hour. The spell was meant for one pillow. It caught a cooper, three choir boys, a mule, and a visiting cleric who was, witnesses say, halfway through a sermon on the virtues of wakefulness. He finished the sentence in his sleep.

"I found three of them stacked by the door like firewood," said Hilde, a turnip farmer. "One was snoring in rhyme." The Sleeping Mule has since put a sign on its cellar door asking sleepers not to nap on the barrels.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said Chapter 9 regards the incident as "a scheduled rest, recently unscheduled." He added that Level Seven of the Undermaw will open next tenday. Nobody laughed, because everyone was asleep or nearly so.

Now for the science, friends. The old herbals say a tired body mends best on a full night's sleep, and the temple studies agree: adults who sleep seven to nine hours catch fewer colds and cough less. The magic kind of sleep, however, does not count. Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor of Chapter 9 confirmed that the sleepers woke feeling "exactly as tired as before," which is the trouble with borrowed rest. It leaves you nothing to give back.

The 57 were all awake by the following noon, with only a stiff neck apiece and, in the cooper's case, a barrel-shaped crease on his face. Shieldwall Mutual says napping is covered, but only the voluntary kind.

So here is my advice. Go to bed at your usual hour, spend the extra one honestly, and leave the spellbook shut. Barley and mushroom soup, thick with thyme, is the proper nightcap. I would suggest my friend Nyx try it too, though first Nyx should go outside and see a morning that came by itself.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Hour Nobody Spent
hook.text: Fifty townsfolk lie asleep after a botched spell and will not wake until the apprentice who cast it finds the counter-ritual. His master, a cranky hedge wizard, wants the party to fetch the ingredients before the Reeve notices.

npc.name: Ferrin Quill
npc.want: To undo his spell before anyone finds out whose it was.
npc.secret: He copied the spell wrong from his master's notes on purpose, hoping to impress him.

location.name: The Drowsy Hearth
location.text: An inn where every guest is already asleep, snoring in perfect time. The innkeeper is the only one awake and refuses to let anyone near the stairs.

campaign.rumor: They say the sleepers are all dreaming the same dream, and it is about turnips.

articles.title: Unidentified Ring Sold for 40 gp, Resold at 1,800 gp
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: A party sold an unidentified ring of protection for 40 gp because nobody cast identify, then saw it priced at 1,800 gp. Barnaby has done the sums.
articles.social: A party sold a plain-looking ring for 40 gp on Monday. By Tuesday it sat in the same shop window at 1,800 gp, and it was a ring of protection. The identify spell would have cost them 100 gp for the pearl. Would you have paid the pearl, or taken the 40 gp and walked?
articles.content:
The Hollow Lanterns, a four-member adventuring party out of the Undermaw, sold an unidentified ring to a Brindlemoor curio dealer on Monday for 40 gp. On Tuesday it was in his window as a ring of protection, priced at 1,800 gp. The difference is 1,760 gp, or 37,647 loaves on the current Loaf Index, which prices a loaf at 4.675 cp. (I have checked that. Four times.)

The ring came off a skeleton on Level Two. The party's wizard, Isolde Fernwhistle, owned a spell of identify but not the pearl it needs, which must be worth 100 gp and is consumed in the casting. A temple will cast it for a fee, but the temple was closed for a feast day. "We were tired and the ring was ugly," said Fernwhistle. "It was a little green. Nobody wanted to carry a green ring for a week."

The dealer, Odo Quillon, paid 40 gp, or 10 gp a head. That is 214 loaves each, which is a perfectly decent supper allowance for the week. Quillon cast identify that same afternoon, on the ring, with a pearl he buys by the dozen. He then priced it at what a ring of protection fetches in Brindlemoor, 1,800 gp, a figure that is 45 times what he paid. "I offered a fair price for what I was told it was," he said. "They told me it was a green ring."

Here is the arithmetic, and I would like everyone seated for it. Had the party waited a day and bought the pearl, they would have spent 100 gp, or 2,139 loaves, and held a ring worth 1,800 gp. After the pearl they would be 1,700 gp ahead of where they stand. Instead they are 40 gp up, and 1,760 gp behind the man who bought from them. Quillon's margin on one afternoon and one pearl, if the ring sells, is 1,660 gp. That is more than the Pellam Isles clerks I know earn in a year. (Four times.)

The Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, says identification is "a personal responsibility" and that its standard form for selling loot says, in small print, "as seen." Fernwhistle has seen the form. She said she wishes she had seen it Monday. The party spent its 40 gp on a round at the tavern and a bandage, and returned to the shop Tuesday to look at the ring in the window. They did not go in. Fernwhistle reports they stood outside for eleven minutes. This is the same price pattern behind a potion of healing now costing 56 gp: the person who knows what a thing is always sells it for more than the person who found it.

My aunt Marigold keeps her savings in a boot, and the boot has never once been sold for less than it was worth, because everyone can see what a boot is. I used to laugh at her.

What this means for your pantry: a 100 gp pearl is 2,139 loaves, and an unidentified ring is a lottery ticket. Buy the pearl, or ask the temple, before you sell anything green.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Ring in the Window
hook.text: The party sold a trinket they never identified, and a dealer is now asking forty times the price. The original owners want it back before a noble buys it, and the dealer will only sell at the full price.

npc.name: Odo Quillon
npc.want: To keep buying unidentified loot cheaply without anyone learning his pearl supplier.
npc.secret: He buys identify pearls in bulk from a temple acolyte who skims them from the offering box.

location.name: Quillon's Green Window
location.text: A cramped curio shop with one display window and a hand-lettered sign reading 'We Buy As Seen.' The window items are all lit by a single continual flame.

campaign.rumor: They say the dealer has never bought a magic item he could not name before he paid, and that he lies about this on purpose.

articles.title: Potion Testers Strike After Polymorph Batch Makes Newts of 9
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Nine apprentice potion testers in Brindlemoor struck Monday after a polymorph batch turned them into newts for a day. They want hazard pay.
articles.social: Nine potion taste-testers in Brindlemoor walked off Monday after an untested batch turned them into newts for a day. They are paid 2 silver a vial and want hazard pay. The shop's owner calls the newt hours a development opportunity. Would you sip the unlabeled vial for 2 silver?
articles.content:
Nine apprentice potion testers in Brindlemoor went on strike Monday. The reason is a polymorph batch that turned all of them into newts for most of Sunday.

The testers work at Dunmallow's Tinctures on Tanner's Row. Their job is to drink each new potion before it is sold and say what happens. Pay is 2 silver a vial. Nobody has ever written down what the pay is for if the answer is "I am a newt."

"I woke up on a lily pad in the cellar," said Wenna Thistlebrook, a taste-tester for three years. "I had no hands. I could not even write down my symptoms. That is a safety problem." She was a newt for fourteen hours. She says the worst part was the flies, which she found delicious, and which she wants it understood she does not approve of.

The shop calls the incident "an unplanned exploration of the amphibian wellness space." That means it turned nine workers into newts. Proprietor Hobb Dunmallow told reporters the batch was labeled "Mild Tonic, Possibly Cherry." He said the label was a draft.

The testers want three things. First, hazard pay of 6 silver a vial for any potion with no label. Second, a cleric on the premises who is awake. Third, a rule that a tester who becomes an animal is paid for the animal hours, because a newt is still on the clock, whatever else it is.

"They offered us a cheese plate," said Orrin Pellmere, a tester who spent Sunday as the cellar's second-largest newt. "Then they remembered we were newts and took it back. I want to be clear that I could have eaten the cheese."

Brindlemoor has watched this shop closely before. The pavement outside is still slightly purple from last spring. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said her office is "aware of the newts" and has asked both sides to meet before Thursday. She said she hoped to avoid a second polymorph situation, though she conceded that this would depend on who is allowed to touch the vials.

The strike is forty-eight hours old and the shop has sold nothing. Customers who arrived Monday found a picket line of nine wet humans in blankets and one very small newt who would not say whether he was on strike or just lost. The testers have lent him a sign.

Dunmallow says he can hire replacements by Wednesday. The testers answer that every replacement will want to know what is in the vial. "That is the whole trouble," said Thistlebrook. "Somebody has to be the one who does not know."

A proper lunch break, a cleric who is awake, and pay for the newt hours. It is not much to ask. The guildmasters get a cloak for that.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Mild Tonic Mix-Up
hook.text: A potion shop's testers are on strike after an unlabeled polymorph batch, and a few vials from that batch were sold before anyone noticed. The shopkeeper hires the party to find the buyers quietly before someone becomes something worse than a newt.

npc.name: Wenna Thistlebrook
npc.want: Hazard pay and a guarantee that the next vial has a label.
npc.secret: She kept one vial from the batch and has been wondering what a longer polymorph would feel like.

location.name: Dunmallow's Tinctures
location.text: A cramped potion shop with a flooded cellar and a picket line of damp apprentices. Something in the cellar water still answers to its name.

campaign.rumor: They say the Mild Tonic batch was not an accident, and that somebody wanted a lot of newts.

articles.title: Adventuring Party Ambushes Envoy Carrying Their Reward
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: The Lantern & Lye Company ambushed a hooded rider at Quillmarch Bridge. He was Calimshan's envoy, carrying their 600 gp reward. Tension: three siege-days.
articles.social: A four-person adventuring party ambushed a hooded rider on the road near Quillmarch Bridge at dusk. He was Calimshan's envoy, hauling their 600 gold quest reward. The reward is now in a mud puddle, and so is the envoy. If your party jumped the one rider who owed you money, would you call it a misunderstanding or a good opening move?
articles.content:
An adventuring party ambushed a hooded rider on the road outside Quillmarch Bridge at dusk on Fifthday. The rider was the envoy of Calimshan, and he was carrying their 600 gold pieces in quest reward. The Lantern & Lye Company, a party of four, had been hired to clear a cellar of giant rats for the barony of Brackwater. They collected nothing for it until Fifthday, when they collected the envoy.

The facts are short. The envoy rode alone, hooded against the rain, and refused to stop when hailed. Refusing to stop is, by the party's own account, the first rule of being a villain. Their rogue dropped from a branch. Their wizard cast sleep, and the envoy's horse took it hardest. Their cleric asked questions only after the questions had stopped being useful.

"He had a hood," said the party's fighter, Dorrin Valecrest, outside the Brackwater magistrate's hall. "Nobody wears a hood in good faith. Also, he was carrying a very heavy bag, and it jingled." It was their pay. The bag was stamped with the Brackwater seal. The seal was the first clue anyone had looked at.

I interviewed the envoy from a safe distance. He sat on a bench with a blanket, one boot missing. He gave his name as Envoy Haskel Tharn. He expects an apology within the week. He declined to say whether he also expects the 600 gp, which the party has already counted twice and now insists is theirs.

This is where it turns into a siege. Brackwater says the party attacked a foreign diplomat on its soil. Calimshan says the party attacked a diplomat on a Brackwater road, which is a different thing and somehow worse. The party says they were paid late and did the arithmetic themselves. Tension stands at three siege-days. It was zero at breakfast.

Handshake review: the envoy and Dorrin Valecrest shook on a truce. Firm, one second, wet. Dagger detected, under the fighter's own cloak. It was returned to its owner.

A parley is scheduled at Quillmarch Bridge for Sixthday, where the bridge troll has already announced a toll for "armed company, and one horse that is not doing well." Brackwater will bring its magistrate. Calimshan will bring a lawyer and a fresh horse. The party will bring their invoice and, according to the cleric, a card.

I like an honest enemy. The party is not that. They are four people who ambushed their own paymaster and called it due diligence. Still, they were upfront about the part where they did it. The photo opportunity afterward, in which the party posed beside the envoy for a Brackwater clerk's sketch, I did not enjoy. I ate a field ration and watched the road.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Paymaster on the Road
hook.text: The party's patron sends them to escort a hooded courier carrying their own reward to town, but a rival company has been told the courier is a bandit and plans to ambush him. The party must reach the courier first, or take the blame and the bruises.

npc.name: Haskel Tharn
npc.want: A written apology and a replacement horse.
npc.secret: He is quietly relieved to be robbed, since the bag held a forged seal he was afraid to deliver.

location.name: The Wet Mile
location.text: A muddy stretch of road before a river crossing where every traveler is stopped at least once. Ambush sites are rented by the hour from a farmer who never seems to be home.

campaign.rumor: They say the hooded rider wasn't the envoy at all, and the real one is still sitting in a bush two miles back.

articles.title: Mimic Chest Opened Four Times After Party Splits Up
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: The Fourth Attempt split up to cover more ground on Level 6. All four corridors reached the same mimic chest, and all four members opened it alone.
articles.social: The Fourth Attempt split up on Level 6 to cover more ground. All four corridors led to the same room, and each member opened the same chest alone. It was a mimic, and it ate in shifts. The fighter is down to 6 hit points. Would you have split up, or held the door?
articles.content:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 6 — The Fourth Attempt split up at a four-way junction yesterday to cover more ground, and all four of them ended up opening the same mimic. The chest, a handsome iron-banded thing in a dead-end room, was reached by each corridor in turn, and nobody was there to say what the last three had already learned.

The reasoning was sound on paper. The party's ranger, whose last navigational idea cost nine hours, proposed one corridor each, "to cover four times the ground." The fighter agreed. The wizard agreed. The party's bard, who asked to be named, agreed loudly, then went the wrong way on purpose to avoid the lecture.

The corridors were a loop. Chapter 9's map shows four branches and one room. I have the map. I rolled poorly and believed it.

The box score, in order of arrival: the ranger, first in at the ten-minute mark, found the chest and a note on its lid reading "Free." He opened it. Mimic. Ranger down to 7 hit points, and stuck. The wizard arrived twelve minutes later, saw a ranger-shaped lump in a chest, and cast detect magic on the ranger. The chest ate the wizard's spell focus. The wizard is at 4 hit points and has a sore wrist.

The fighter came third. "There was a chest, with two of my friends in it," he told me from a stretcher. "I thought, it's a trap, and I'm the one to deal with it." He is at 6 hit points. He died once before, and Shieldwall Mutual has already asked whether this counts as a second pre-existing condition. The bard arrived last, took one look, and sat on the floor and played a ballad. The mimic let him finish. Nobody has explained this, and I am not going to press it.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, was waiting at the junction with the mule. He read the afternoon's clause aloud. "Splitting the party is permitted," he said. "Opening the same chest four times is a separate item." The hirelings, who took the one route that was not a loop, were unharmed and a day ahead on pay. The mule is, once again, at full health.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the map is "on track" and that the loop will be listed as a "scenic option" in the next printing. Chapter 9 has also confirmed that the chest is a monster, per its own hazard pay ruling, and that the party has no claim on the loot inside it. The loot inside it is the wizard's spell focus.

The ranger has asked to be released from the chest by the end of the week. Pottage says that is a negotiation. My ninth ten-foot pole of the season is still in there, too.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: Four Doors, One Chest
hook.text: Four corridors in an old dungeon all end in the same dead-end room with a single iron-banded chest, which is a mimic. The party must find the one corridor that is not a loop before the chest finishes the previous expedition's survivors.

npc.name: Tilda Brannock
npc.want: She wants the party to confirm her map before the guild sees the errors.
npc.secret: She drew the loop on purpose, to keep rivals away from a vault.

location.name: The Loop Room
location.text: A dead-end chamber that four separate corridors reach, with a single chest in the middle. Scorch marks and ten-foot pole stubs line the floor.

campaign.rumor: They say a chest down there has eaten more explorers than the dragon ever did, and it hasn't even bothered to learn anybody's name.

articles.title: Rope Trick Pod Launches at 90 gp; Exit Costs Extra
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Cinderlatch's new 90 gp Rope Trick Pod opens an extradimensional room for eight hours. Nyx moved in for a weekend. Four eyes, and a landlord.
articles.social: Cinderlatch just launched a 90 gp Rope Trick Pod that opens a private extradimensional room. Nyx moved in for a weekend and learned the door is a subscription. Byte now sells hallway access in ad copy. Would you rent a room that charges for the way out?
articles.content:
OKAY. The Cinderlatch Rope Trick Pod is out in Brindlemoor shops today at 90 gp, and it is a rope trick you can carry in a satchel. Climb the rope, step into an extradimensional room for up to eight hours, and nobody can follow you in. I moved in for the weekend. I have notes!

The unboxing alone is worth the price. The pod is a brass cylinder with a rune-ring, a coil of enchanted rope, and a quick-start card that says 'Please do not read the other card.' I read the other card. It is the terms of service, and it is eleven feet long.

Setup took four minutes. The room itself is lovely: a cozy chamber, one cot, one lantern, no windows, and a mana throughput so smooth that my tea stayed hot for six hours. Runic latency on the rope was effectively zero. I pulled it up after me, exactly as promised, and for the first time in my life I was in a place where no one could ask me for a review.

Then the pod chimed. Hour seven brought a gentle notice: 'Your free hallway has expired.' It turns out the base 90 gp covers the room, and the way out is the Cinderlatch Egress tier at 4 sp a day. Without it, the rope retracts when the timer ends and you simply stand where the room used to be. Which is, I confirmed, a pantry in Cinderlatch's shipping office. Twice.

Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, offered a review of his own. 'Upgrade to Egress Plus today,' he said, from inside the pod, where I had not invited him. I did not know he had been in there. He had been in there for the whole weekend. He has a cot now.

I asked Cinderlatch's launch spokesman, a smiling man named Dobb Wrenfield, whether charging for the exit was fair. 'It is not an exit,' he said. 'It is a premium egress experience.' Then he asked me to step away from the demo model, which I was still standing in.

My rival Brother Wendell Tumbleberry has already written that I should 'touch grass' instead of renting a pocket dimension. Wendell, the room has a lantern and no grass, and it is the best weekend I have had all year. You would hate it. Please do not buy one.

Verdict: the room is superb, the rope is smooth, the subscription is a crime, and I have already paid for the Egress tier. Four out of five beholder eyes. The fifth is locked behind Egress Plus.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Gold spent: 94. Pantries entered: 2. Familiars evicted: 0. Eyebrows: fine, for once.

hook.title: The Pantry That Wasn't
hook.text: A merchant swears her rented extradimensional room dumped her into a locked storeroom owned by a rival, and the rival accuses her of theft. The party must find out who really keeps opening the room's exit into other people's pantries before the magistrate hangs the wrong tenant.

npc.name: Dobb Wrenfield
npc.want: To keep the egress fee out of the courtroom.
npc.secret: He sold the pantry's key to a thief who uses the pod as a smuggling route.

location.name: The Cinderlatch Shipping Office
location.text: A stout brick warehouse by the docks, stacked with sealed crates. Its back pantry has a rope hanging in the air, and nobody will admit it was always there.

campaign.rumor: They say the rope trick rooms are all one room, and that's why the cot is always warm.

articles.title: Mimic Ballot Box Eats 31 Votes in Brindlemoor By-Election
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A mimic posing as the ballot box swallowed 31 ballots in a Brindlemoor Burgess by-election. The Council must now rule on whether the mimic voted.
articles.social: A mimic posing as the ballot box swallowed 31 ballots in Brindlemoor's Burgess by-election on Tuesday. Returning Officer Haldis Brume noticed when the box asked for a second helping. Two Burgesses want the mimic counted as a voter. Should the box's ballot count?
articles.content:
A mimic posing as the ballot box in Tuesday's Brindlemoor by-election swallowed 31 ballots before anyone noticed, the Returning Officer confirmed. The Burgess Council, which had only just recovered from the doppelganger who held two seats, has called a recess to discuss it.

The box had been in the Guildhall cellar since the last by-election, where it was labeled "Ballot Box (Oak)" and left unattended. Returning Officer Haldis Brume says she first grew suspicious when it asked for a second helping. "Ballot boxes are not supposed to say anything," she told the Chamber. "Certainly not 'more.'"

Procedure matters here, so I will state it. Under the Brindlemoor Charter, a ballot is valid once it is placed in the box. It is silent on what happens when the box places the voter in itself. Three voters were recovered, damp but willing to vote again. The other 28 ballots are, in the Returning Officer's words, "in the box, in a manner of speaking."

The gentleman from Tanner's Row moved that the 31 ballots be counted as cast, since the box had acted as a lawful receptacle. The lady from the Mill Ward moved that they be struck, since the box had acted as a lawful meal. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor, chairing, noted that she was "aware of the mimic" and asked both members to stop shouting at the furniture.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the box has been seen at four prior by-elections. "It always seemed heavy," the courtier said. "We assumed that was democracy."

The Council's tally for the session now stands at Promises Made, nine, and Promises Kept, none. The Chamber did pass a resolution to inspect all future furniture, which was drafted in two hours and vetoed by a chair. The chair was found to be a mimic as well. It has been removed, and the vote was retaken standing.

Two Burgesses have asked that the mimic be counted as a voter in its own right. Its ballot, they note, was the only one cast with total conviction. The Council's counsel advised that the Charter requires a voter to be a resident, a signatory, and, by the strictest reading, not a cellar. The ghost who filibustered for thirteen days offered to speak in the mimic's favor and was gently asked to sit.

For now the box sits in the Chamber, under guard, with a sign reading "Do Not Feed." Eleven Burgesses have already fed it a motion. The motion carried. Nobody read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Hungry Ballot Box
hook.text: A town's election box has eaten 28 ballots, and the losing candidate swears the missing votes would have changed the result. The mayor will pay the party to open the box, if it can be done without losing the box.

npc.name: Haldis Brume
npc.want: To get the ballots back before the Council finds out how many were hers.
npc.secret: She fed the box a few ballots herself, to test it, before she understood it was alive.

location.name: The Guildhall Cellar
location.text: A damp storeroom full of furniture nobody has sat on in years. Several pieces are slightly too warm.

campaign.rumor: They say the box only eats ballots for the candidate who promised to cut the cellar rent.

articles.title: Wizard Casts Fireball in Tavern Back Room, Burns Own Party
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A wizard cast fireball in a 10-foot tavern back room on Fish Street during a brawl and the blast got his whole adventuring party. Allegedly.
articles.social: A wizard cast fireball in a 10-by-12-foot tavern back room on Fish Street during a brawl. It hit the brawlers, and it also hit all four of his own party. The cleric said he asked everyone to step back, and the wizard says he heard 'step in'. Your wizard has the spell ready and the room is tiny. Do you cast it anyway?
articles.content:
At roughly the third bell after midnight, a wizard allegedly cast fireball inside a 10-foot-by-12-foot back room at the Leaking Boot on Fish Street, catching a card-table brawl and all four members of his own adventuring party, the Gilded Ladles. The Constabulary counted nine singed patrons, one melted card deck, and a cat that left through the ceiling.

'He said it would be fine,' said Dunstan Perrywick, a cooper, who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'He said the spell goes where you point it. Then he pointed it at the middle of the room, which is where the room was.' The turkey leg survived. Perrywick says this is the only part of the evening that went to plan.

The Ladles had gone into the back room to settle a bill dispute, and the brawl started when a rival table accused them of marking cards with a wand. Witnesses say the wizard, Orrin Tuck, shouted a warning. The cleric says it was 'everyone step back.' Tuck says it was 'everyone step in, I have a plan.' Nobody has produced the plan.

The blast filled the entire room, because that is what fireball allegedly does when the room is small. The fighter lost his eyebrows and half a cloak. The rogue lost her hat and, briefly, her faith in wizards. The cleric healed herself first, which the party is now calling 'a tactical decision' and which the fighter is calling something longer.

Keeper Dolly Ashgate says the fire also took the back-room door, a shelf of pickles, and 14 stools, for a total of 62 gold pieces in damage. 'Fire spread to the pickle shelf and the pickles screamed,' she said. 'I don't know why. I've never asked.' She has billed the party jointly. The party has asked who pays for a wizard's share. The Constabulary has said it is not a legal question, it is a seating chart.

Also, there was a lovely little silver spoon on the floor of the wreckage and I looked at it for a while. Anyway.

Tuck was found outside holding his hat, which was on fire. 'In my defense, the room was bigger in my head,' he said. Asked about the earlier Undermaw corridor fireball that also hurt his friends, Tuck said the two were 'unrelated, mostly.' The fighter, who is allegedly still smoking, asked this paper to print that the Ladles will vote on a new rule: no fireball indoors, no fireball in anything with a door, and no fireball if the cleric is holding a drink.

The Leaking Boot reopens Thursday with a new door and a sign reading 'FIREBALL: HALL ONLY.' The pickles are expected to recover. Allegedly.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Fireball Fee
hook.text: A tavern keeper wants the party to find out which of two rival groups really started a back-room brawl, because the one who did owes 62 gp and the other has friends in the guild. If the party is also in the room when it kicks off, someone should probably check the spell slots first.

npc.name: Dolly Ashgate
npc.want: To be paid 62 gold pieces for the damage and to never see another wand at a card table.
npc.secret: She quietly sold the rival table a marked deck so there would be a brawl to bill for.

location.name: The Leaking Boot Back Room
location.text: A 10 by 12 foot card room behind a tavern kitchen, with one door, no windows, and a scorched ceiling shaped like a cat.

campaign.rumor: They say the pickles in the Boot scream because the cellar is haunted, but the keeper swears it was only the vinegar.

articles.title: Owlbear Union Vote at Hootline Ends 38 to 2, Sterling Rattled
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: The owlbear couriers at Hootline Couriers voted 38 to 2 to form a union on Monday. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a disruption of the workforce.
articles.social: The owlbear couriers at Hootline voted 38 to 2 to unionize on Monday. Their first demand is two goats per shift and no more wearing the company hat. Founder Marla Quillfeather called it a pivot. Would you cross that picket line?
articles.content:
The owlbear couriers at Hootline Couriers voted 38 to 2 on Monday to form a union, the first owlbear union in the history of the Brindlemoor exchange. The two holdouts were reportedly asleep. Founder and Chief Feather Officer Marla Quillfeather, whose firm was last week up 60% in its debut, called the result "a pivot toward stakeholder engagement." Her stock fell 11% by noon.

Let me say this plainly, friends: I do not love unions. I love growth. But I also love a good story, and this one has a lot of claws.

The union, styled the Amalgamated Order of Hooting Couriers, filed three demands with Chapter 9. Two goats per shift. An end to the mandatory company hat, which Hootline insists is a "brand halo" and the owlbears insist is a bucket. And a clause that parcels must be delivered "in whole, not in part," a reference to what organizers called "the Thursday situation."

Quillfeather held a press stand outside the Hootline warehouse on Tanner's Row. "Our owlbears are not employees," she said. "They are partners in a gig-based ecosystem." Behind her, an owlbear named Biscuit the shop steward ate her podium. I cannot confirm whether it was a negotiating tactic, but I would have called it one.

Rightsizing the adventuring party is a tool I defend. Rightsizing an owlbear is a tool I am told is called "a hand." Hootline's board has floated replacing the whole fleet with pigeons. Analyst Dunwick Harl of the Brindlemoor exchange noted pigeons carry only a twelfth of the payload, but "they do not have opinions." Within an hour, the pigeons had formed a committee of their own.

Some will say a 38 to 2 vote means management failed to listen. I say it means management found an extremely engaged workforce. When I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a gala in a hot-air balloon, he told me, "Sterling, a worker who bites is a worker who cares." I did not understand him then. I understand him now, and my left sleeve is shorter for it.

The owlbears have set a strike deadline of Friday. Until then, parcels continue to arrive, mostly. Reeve Fennick says the town is "aware of the owlbears" and has asked residents to leave goats on their porches as a goodwill measure. Several porches have since been entered.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Never put a hat on a workforce that can eat the hat.
  • A 38 to 2 vote is just a very large focus group.
  • Stock down 11% is a buying opportunity if you are very brave.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Picket Line Bites
hook.text: A courier firm's owlbear workers have gone on strike and parcels with vital goods are stuck in a warehouse the owlbears guard. The owner offers the party gold to negotiate or sneak the cargo out before Friday.

npc.name: Brenna Tuckwell
npc.want: To win the owlbears two goats a shift and a hatless contract.
npc.secret: She has been quietly paid by the firm's rival to keep the strike going.

location.name: The Hooting Yard
location.text: A fenced warehouse lot stacked with parcels and one enormous feather-lined shed. The goats tied outside are always one fewer than yesterday.

campaign.rumor: They say the pigeons are the ones who really started the union, and the owlbears just got the credit.

articles.title: Rogue Licks Glowing Ooze; Adventuring Party Now Lit Up
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: A rogue licked glowing ooze on Undermaw Level Six to see what it was. His tongue now glows, and Brother Wendell says friends, please stop tasting walls.
articles.social: A rogue in the adventuring party the Lantern Pigs licked glowing ooze on Undermaw Level Six to check what it was. Eleven minutes later his tongue lit up like a lantern, and three kobold ambushes found the party by it. Sister Odda dimmed it to a candle. What is the dumbest thing your character has ever put in their mouth?
articles.content:
Friends, an adventuring party called the Lantern Pigs came up from Undermaw Level Six on Tuesday with a rogue whose tongue glows. Pip Nettlewhistle, a halfling, licked a patch of blue-green ooze on a dungeon wall "to check what it was." Eleven minutes later, his tongue began to shine through his cheek like a lantern behind a curtain.

The old herbals have a single rule on this, and it is a short one: never taste what you cannot name. A Brindlemoor Infirmary tally agrees, counting 19 wall-licking cases on the Undermaw ledger since spring, which is 19 more than I would like. Pip said the ooze "looked friendly." It was, in fairness, a gray ooze that had been leaning on a glow-moss colony, so the shine was only borrowed. The sting was not.

The trouble was how well the glow carried. Pip is the party's scout and sneaks for a living. Within the hour, three separate kobold ambush crews found the Lantern Pigs by following what they described as "a very rude blue tongue in the dark." Party cleric Sister Odda Marsh says Pip tried to whisper past a sentry with his mouth shut. His cheeks lit up and the sentry waved.

Sister Odda cast lesser restoration at the Level Four rest stop, which dimmed the tongue from a lantern to a candle. The rest, she says, has to wear off on its own, about four days. Pip may not scout until then, and for the duration he is to be known on the party roll as the Torch. He is said to be taking it well. He is also not taking sips of anything out of the water barrel.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the incident "a complimentary lighting upgrade" and said the guild had no plan to relabel the ooze. "We do not discourage tasting," he told this paper. "We discourage tasting without a permit." A permit costs eleven silver and, to be clear, covers no medical care.

You may recall that the Fourth Attempt drank nine unidentified potions last week, and one of them floats. A party that cannot keep its mouth shut is a healer's whole winter. So here is the rule, friends, as plain as a spoon: if it glows, you look at it. If it drips, you walk around it. If you have to ask a friend what it is, the friend should not be near it either.

For a tongue that has seen better days, I recommend a plain chicken-and-ginger broth, warm, not hot, with a slice of lemon to cut the memory of ooze. Three coppers, and no permit required. My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that identifies slime by photograph. Go outside, Nyx, and take a photograph of a tree.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Torch Cannot Sneak
hook.text: A scout licked something glowing and now his tongue lights up the whole corridor, with four days to wear off and a dungeon to cross. The party must get him through a kobold warren by dark, or find the cure before the sentries do.

npc.name: Odda Marsh
npc.want: To get her scout's tongue to dim before the party is ambushed again.
npc.secret: She dimmed it halfway on purpose, because the glow has been leading them to treasure.

location.name: The Level Four Rest Stop
location.text: A dry alcove with a cot, a barrel, and a sign reading Please Do Not Lick. Someone has crossed out Please.

campaign.rumor: They say a glow-lipped halfling can read in the dark if he talks loud enough, and he talks loud enough.

articles.title: Party Tips Bard 500 gp Pearl, Mistaking It for 1 sp
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party tipped a tavern bard a 500 gp black pearl, thinking it was 1 sp, and then paid 400 gp to get it back. Barnaby has done the sums.
articles.social: A party tipped a tavern bard in Brindlemoor what they thought was 1 sp. It was a 500 gp black pearl from the hoard, a tip 5,000 times too large. They then offered 5 gp, 20 gp and 60 gp for her "keepsake" without once saying why. Would you confess at the bar, or keep bidding for a silver piece?
articles.content:
An adventuring party called the Crooked Ladder tipped a bard at the Sleeping Mule Tavern on Monday night with what they believed was a silver piece, and it was a black pearl worth 500 gp. The tip is 5,000 times the usual one, which is a silver, and on the Loaf Index, at 4.675 cp a loaf, it comes to 10,695 loaves instead of two. (I have checked that. Four times.)

The pearl came out of the Undermaw that afternoon with the rest of the hoard. Nobody cast identify, a habit that also cost one party a ring sold for 40 gp yesterday. The party's rogue, Cassian Brewhouse, told this paper he reached into a pouch in the dark and "felt something round and small, like a coin." The bard, Dorrie Haverstock, a halfling who plays the hurdy-gurdy, said she knew it was a pearl because "it rolled off the table and sang."

The party, five adventurers in all, noticed the mistake at the next round, when they counted the hoard and found a pearl-shaped gap. None of them wished to say so out loud. Captain Ysolde Marrowgate told the Gazette the group would "not be discussing the pearl," and then, on being asked which pearl, discussed it for eleven minutes.

What followed was a bidding war against themselves. The party first offered Haverstock 5 gp for the silver piece, citing sentiment. She declined. They offered 20 gp, saying it was an heirloom. She declined. They offered 60 gp, and Brewhouse added that the coin had belonged to his grandmother. "Your grandmother's coin was round and loud," Haverstock said. "This was round and expensive."

Here are the numbers. By midnight the party had offered 85 gp across three bids, plus a round for the house, for a coin the bard was entitled to keep. Haverstock took the pearl to a Tanner's Row pawnbroker, who valued it at 500 gp, and then named her own price: 400 gp. The party paid. That is 8,556 loaves to undo a mistake that cost 2 loaves to make, or 80% of the pearl's value, against the 10% a money changer charges to turn copper into silver. Haverstock now has 400 gp and a ballad in progress called The Silver That Wasn't.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said the town has no rule against a tip that is too large. "We are aware of the pearl," she said. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said that the whole matter was "on track" and that tipping would remain voluntary.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, keeps her tipping coins in a separate sock so she cannot mistake them. I used to laugh at her. I now own six socks.

What this means for your pantry: look at what you hand over in the dark, and if a tip rolls and sings, it is not a silver.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Pearl in the Tip Jar
hook.text: A bard at a busy tavern has been tipped a black pearl by a nervous party who keep offering to buy it back at ever-higher prices. Someone has noticed, and a gem thief is watching the bard's room.

npc.name: Dorrie Haverstock
npc.want: To keep the pearl long enough to finish a ballad about it, and then sell it for the best price.
npc.secret: She has already guessed whose hoard it came from and is quietly planning to return it for a reward.

location.name: The Gilded Gutter
location.text: A crowded tavern with a bard's corner raised on a barrel. The tip jar is a chamber pot and no one knows why.

campaign.rumor: I heard the bard got a pearl as a tip and she's keeping it in her boot, or maybe her instrument.

articles.title: Wizard's Familiar Files Grievance Over Trap Duty, Wants Pay
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: A weasel familiar sent first into every trapped room by his adventuring party filed a grievance with Chapter 9 Tuesday. He wants breaks and hazard pay.
articles.social: A weasel familiar named Mr. Nib has filed a grievance after being sent first into 41 trapped rooms in one delve. He wants a break every hour and hazard pay of 6 copper per trap. His wizard says he is basically a pet. Would you pay the weasel?
articles.content:
A wizard's familiar filed a grievance with Chapter 9 of the Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild on Tuesday. He wants breaks and hazard pay for being sent first into every trapped corridor and room on his adventuring party's last delve.

The familiar is a weasel called Mr. Nib. His wizard is Orsolya Venn. Their party, the Muddy Boot Four, entered the Undermaw last week and met 41 trapped rooms. Mr. Nib went into all 41. He was struck by a dart, a swinging blade, a falling net, and what he calls 'a floor with opinions.'

'He's a familiar,' said Venn. 'It's in the name. It's basically a pet.' That means she sent a living creature ahead of the party and called it a job description.

Mr. Nib wrote his own grievance, in tiny script, over three nights. It lists four demands: a ten-minute rest every hour, hazard pay of 6 copper per trap, a say in the marching order, and a rope tied to him that someone actually holds. The rope is the sore point. 'I was told there was a rope,' he wrote. 'There was a knot.'

Chapter 9 says it has never paid a familiar, because familiars are classed as equipment. Mr. Nib's steward, Dessa Hollowbrook, disagrees. 'Equipment doesn't have opinions,' said Hollowbrook, a trap-line steward for eleven years. 'Equipment doesn't ask for water at the third door. He asked. Twice. Nobody answered.'

Gredwin Marsh, a hireling porter who walked behind the weasel, backs him. 'I carried the lantern. I watched him go in front,' said Marsh. 'Forty-one rooms. At the pressure plate in room thirty he looked back at me. I will think about that look for the rest of my days.' Marsh was one of the sixty-one porters who struck over pit traps last week. He says the familiars are next, and the Guild should see it coming.

The Muddy Boot Four argue that a familiar's bond is not employment. Venn says Mr. Nib shares in every spell she casts and eats from her own plate. Mr. Nib says the plate is a saucer, and that he has had the same saucer since spring.

The sums are not hard. Forty-one traps at 6 copper is 246 copper, about twenty-five silver for a week of near-death. The party's haul from the delve was 900 gold. Venn kept the weasel's share in her pocket and called it a bond dividend. That means she kept it.

A hearing is set for Friday at Chapter 9. Mr. Nib will attend, sitting on a clerk's stack of forms, and has asked that nobody send him through the door first. The Muddy Boot Four have offered a compromise: a thicker saucer.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Weasel Walks Out
hook.text: The party's scout-familiar refuses to enter the next trapped chamber until the party agrees to rest breaks and a fair share of treasure. The wizard insists the familiar is property, and a guild steward is watching the argument with great interest.

npc.name: Dessa Hollowbrook
npc.want: She wants the guild to recognize familiars and hirelings as paid workers with breaks.
npc.secret: She is secretly paid by a rival outfitter to keep adventurers distracted by labor disputes.

location.name: The Forty-First Room
location.text: A trapped chamber at the end of a long corridor, its floor a patchwork of pressure plates and faded chalk marks. Every plate has a tiny paw print, and one of them is still warm.

campaign.rumor: They say the weasel isn't a familiar at all, but a cursed apprentice who signed the wrong scroll.

articles.title: Gelatinous Cube Hosted Varnholt-Pellam Parley as 'Glass Room'
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: A gelatinous cube posing as a glass conference room hosted three days of Varnholt and Pellam Isles talks. The treaty dissolved. Tension: seven siege-days.
articles.social: A gelatinous cube hosted three days of talks between Varnholt and the Pellam Isles. Delegates took it for a glass conference room. The treaty was signed at dusk and dissolved by dawn, along with one clerk's hat. Would you have sat down in it?
articles.content:
A gelatinous cube, mistaken for a glass-walled conference room, hosted three full days of Varnholt and Pellam Isles peace talks before anyone noticed. Both delegations walked in on Firstday and began to parley. The room was the cube's insides.

The handshake between Varnholt's envoy and the Isles' envoy lasted two seconds. Firm, slightly tingly. No hidden dagger detected. In hindsight, the dagger was the only thing not being digested.

"The walls were very clean," said Odo Tillman, a Varnholt clerk who kept the minutes. "We assumed the Isles valued transparency." By the second day the delegates' buttons had gone missing. By the third, the delegates agreed the missing buttons were a "constructive gesture." Nobody got up to check.

The talks themselves went well, which should have been the clue. Varnholt dropped its berth fee for fishing skiffs. The Isles agreed to stop calling Varnholt's customs ledger "a hobby." Both sides signed the treaty at dusk. By dawn it was a faint stain on the table, which was also the cube. The minutes went the same way, along with three quills and Tillman's hat.

Harbormaster Ilsabet Corvane, who ordered the room drained with a ladle and a fresh round of customs forms, called the discovery "a breach of diplomatic premises." The Isles' envoy called it "a breach of a cube." Both sides now claim the other brought it.

The cube has filed no statement. It remains in the embassy hall, where it has resumed being a room. Delegates were freed when a veteran guardsman cast a mage hand to pull the last envoy out by the collar. He asked that his name not be printed. He said it was the cleanest negotiation of his career, and the wettest.

Whether a treaty signed inside a monster binds anyone is now a legal question. Varnholt's lawyers say the cube was a neutral venue. The Isles' lawyers say it was a party, since it ate the evidence. I say it was the only participant that wanted something clear and went and got it. I respect that. I hate that Ottoline Vex will call it a triumph of the gallery seat, having watched none of it.

Both delegations return to the table Sixthday, in a room confirmed by detect magic to be an ordinary room. Tension holds at seven siege-days. The cube is expected to attend the opening anyway, as the lobby.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Room That Ate the Treaty
hook.text: A peace treaty signed in a glass conference room has dissolved along with the minutes, and both sides blame the other. The party is hired to find a copy before the envoys declare a trade war over a missing signature.

npc.name: Odo Tillman
npc.want: To recover the hat and the minutes, in that order.
npc.secret: He copied the treaty from memory beforehand and has been adding clauses in the margins.

location.name: The Glass Embassy Hall
location.text: A narrow embassy hall with suspiciously spotless walls. Visitors report their buttons going missing in the first hour.

campaign.rumor: They say the cube only agreed to be a room because it was promised a seat at the next round of talks.

articles.title: Bag of Holding Recalled After Hirelings' Wages Go Missing
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: Chapter 9 recalled a batch of bag of holding sacks after the Fourth Attempt's bag gave back everything but the wages. Hit points held; coin did not.
articles.social: Chapter 9 has recalled Batch 7 of the bag of holding after the Fourth Attempt's bag handed back a lantern, a cheese, and a spare mule shoe, but not the hirelings' 212 gold in wages. Deputy Registrar Oddingwick calls the coin 'in transit.' Would you pay into a bag that keeps your wages somewhere else?
articles.content:
THE CHAPTER 9 EQUIPMENT CAGE, GROUND LEVEL, BRINDLEMOOR — Chapter 9 recalled every bag of holding from Batch 7 this morning, after the Fourth Attempt's bag returned a lantern, a wheel of cheese, and one mule shoe, but not the hirelings' wages. The wages came to 212 gold pieces. Nobody has seen them since the party's bursar put them in on Tuesday.

I was in the cage when the bag was turned out on the counter. Hit points on the floor: the fighter at 14, the wizard at 6, the bursar at a bruised 11, because he reached in to the shoulder and something on the other side reached back. Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the sales receipt aloud. 'It says the bag holds everything you put in,' he said. 'It does not say it gives it back. I have been reading the next line for nine years.'

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick called the recall a soft launch of a quality program. He said the coin is 'in transit' and 'on track to be located.' Asked where it was in transit to, he said the bag's interior is 'a matter for the manufacturer,' and the manufacturer is a gnome in Cobblewick who has not answered three ravens. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the bag 'felt different after lunch.' He then described the feeling as 'shifty,' which Chapter 9 has entered as a technical finding.

The recall covers forty-one bags. Chapter 9 asks owners to bring them to the cage, empty if possible, and to stand back while the clerk opens each one with a ten-foot pole. That is the pole I lost today, my fourteenth of the season. It went in and did not come out, and the clerk wrote it up as 'stored.' I rolled poorly on that one. I should have held on to the end.

Shieldwall Mutual says a bag that eats wages is a pre-existing condition of the bag. Reeve Fennick, passing through the cage on her way to something worse, said only, 'We are aware of the bag.' She did order the clerk to post the hours the cage is open, which had not been done, and which turned out to be fewer than the hours posted outside.

The hirelings have filed for their wages with Chapter 9 and are owed a tip regardless. Pottage said the mule, who carried the bag all week, will be paid first, 'since she is the only one who ever saw the inside and kept quiet.' The mule declined to comment and ate part of the receipt.

Owners who cannot make it to the cage may hold their bags upside down over a bucket and shake. Chapter 9 does not recommend this, but notes that three people already have.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: The Bag That Kept the Wages
hook.text: A merchant's bag of holding has swallowed a hireling crew's pay, and the crew will walk off a caravan job unless it is found. Someone on the other side of the bag has been reaching back, and the party must decide whether to open it.

npc.name: Dunmar Quillfeather
npc.want: To quietly buy back the recalled bags before anyone opens one.
npc.secret: He sold the batch knowing the stitching opened onto a pocket shared with a stranger's vault.

location.name: The Equipment Cage
location.text: A caged counter in a guild hall where recalled gear is checked and shelved. Whatever goes into the back shelves comes out slightly later than it went in.

campaign.rumor: They say the bag opens onto somebody's pantry, and he has been eating the cheese.

articles.title: Speak with Dead Wasted: Party Burns All 5 Questions
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: A party cast Speak with Dead on the one clerk who knew the vault code, then spent all five questions bickering. Nyx was in the room.
articles.social: A party cast Speak with Dead on the only clerk who knew the vault code. Five questions later they had the number seven, a gap, and a dead man saying 'Stairs.' Nobody got the code. Which question would you have asked first?
articles.content:
The Brass Kettle Brotherhood, a four-member adventuring party out of Brindlemoor, cast Speak with Dead on Tuesday night on the one clerk who knew the combination to the Dunwick Bullion Vault, and used all five questions without learning it. I was there as an embedded reviewer, because a launch is a launch, and I have never been so excited to watch something go so wrong!

The setup was perfect. The clerk, Gerrit Sallowmere, had fallen down his own stairs a day earlier. The wizard, Ferrin, had the spell prepared and a fresh pouch of ash. The mana throughput was gorgeous. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, watched from my shoulder and said, 'Ask smarter, with Brass Kettle Premium.' He is not wrong, but he is also not helping.

Question one, from Ferrin: 'Do you know the vault code?' Sallowmere said, 'Yes.' This is technically an answer. The cleric, Marga, groaned loudly enough to wake the next barony.

Question two, from Marga, who insisted she was fixing it: 'Do you want to tell us?' Sallowmere said, 'No.' The room went quiet. The rogue, Dib, said it was a very Marga question. Marga said the rogue could ask the next one, then. That is how the third question was spent on a fight about who was allowed to ask the next question.

Question three, from the paladin, Sir Oswin, who had not been following any of this: 'How did you die?' 'Stairs,' said Sallowmere. Everyone already knew that.

Question four finally went to the right topic, which was a relief until the bard, Pip, phrased it as 'What is the code, roughly?' The answer was 'Seven. Then a gap.' Pip wrote it down on his sleeve, which he then forgot he was wearing.

Question five was Ferrin's last chance. 'Is the gap a number?' he asked. 'Yes,' said Sallowmere, and the spell wound down with the sound of a very small door closing. The party now holds a code that starts with seven, continues with a gap, and has not been fully recorded by anyone. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor has declined comment, though her aide was seen adding the Brotherhood to the list of people who shall not be told anything useful in future.

As a product, the spell is stunning. The runic latency is nil. The firmware glyph of the answer is clean. But the user experience depends entirely on the users, and these users argued over the order of questions while the clock ran. Four out of five beholder eyes. I would give five, but I remain loyal to that dead clerk, who answered everything asked of him, honestly and in full.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 0. Arguments witnessed: 6. Digits of vault code recovered: 1.5. Eyebrows: fine.

hook.title: Seven, Then a Gap
hook.text: A party wasted its questions on a dead vault clerk and has only the first digit of a combination. The vault's owner will pay anyone who can recover the rest, from the clerk's old notes, his killer, or a second corpse.

npc.name: Hesper Dunwick
npc.want: To open the vault before her creditors learn it is shut.
npc.secret: She is the only other person who knows the code, and she has forgotten it too.

location.name: The Dunwick Bullion Vault
location.text: A squat stone vault with a dial of twelve numbers and a plaque reading 'Under new management'. The dial is warm, as if recently used by someone who left no tracks.

campaign.rumor: They say Sallowmere hid the rest of the code in the stair carpet, and that is why the stairs killed him.

articles.title: Adventuring Party Sworn to Lord After Coin Pickup Mishap
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A rogue knelt to gather dropped coins in Lord Hask's hall and swore fealty by accident, binding her whole adventuring party to his chores.
articles.social: A rogue dropped eleven silver in Lord Hask's hall, knelt to pick them up, and swore fealty for her entire party. They now owe him forty eggs a month and a nightly goose count. Would you pay the fine or guard the geese?
articles.content:
An adventuring party called the Seventh Lantern was bound this week to the petty obligations of Lord Perrin Hask of Dunnowick Hollow after its rogue, Tamsin Wick, knelt to pick up eleven dropped silver pieces in his hall. Under the hall's custom, a person who kneels on the dais step while the lord says "Who serves?" has sworn fealty. Wick says she heard nothing. The steward says he said it twice.

The gentleman from Dunnowick Hollow, who holds eleven acres and a very large chair, wasted no time. By noon the Lantern's fighter, cleric, and wizard had each received a scroll of duties. By evening they had learned the oath covers "all companions, present or later reunited," a phrase the party's contract with its hireling steward, Ansel Pottage, had not prepared them for.

I have read the scroll. It runs to nine items. The party must supply forty eggs a month, attend the annual hay count, polish the statue of the lord's late father (bronze, life-sized, wearing a hat), and guard his geese from dusk to the second bell. The geese, it should be noted, are not under threat. The lord simply likes them watched.

"I picked up my own money," Wick told this reporter outside the hall, still holding the eleven silver. "Nobody told me the floor had a vote." The party's cleric, Brother Odo Marsh, asked whether a pledge made by accident could be undone by an accidental unpledge. The steward replied that Lord Hask accepts only formal resignations, delivered in person, on a day ending in a hay count.

The Lantern appealed to Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor of Chapter 9, who ruled that she has jurisdiction over dungeons and chairs, but not over lords. The lady from Chapter 9 added that she would, however, keep the file open, since it was already on her desk and she did not want to move it.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake confirmed that the hall's custom dates to the founding, when it was meant to stop beggars from lingering. It has since caught two tax collectors, a bard, and a goat. The goat is still employed.

By my tally, the Lantern's Promises Made now stand at nine, one for each item on the scroll. Promises Kept stand at the egg delivery, which was late and consisted of fourteen eggs and a note. Lord Hask has accepted the note. He is reportedly considering the geese for a promotion.

The party departs for the Undermaw at first light, pending the goose count. Nobody has told the geese.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Floor Has a Vote
hook.text: A PC kneels to grab a dropped coin in a petty lord's hall and unknowingly swears fealty for the whole party. Lord Hask's steward now hands out chores: eggs, geese, a statue to polish. The party must find a legal way out before the duties get in the way of the real quest.

npc.name: Perrin Hask
npc.want: To be treated as important, and to have his geese watched.
npc.secret: He cannot read the oath himself and relies entirely on his steward, who has been quietly adding items for years.

location.name: Dunnowick Hollow Great Hall
location.text: A drafty hall with a raised dais and a single worn step. The step is trapped by custom: anyone kneeling on it while the lord speaks counts as sworn.

campaign.rumor: They say the goat that swore in last spring now holds a higher rank than the steward.

articles.title: Zoning Board Weighs Dragon Hoard Annex on Fish Street
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: A young dragon asked the Brindlemoor zoning board to extend its hoard into a neighbor's cellar. The hearing ran 6 hours. Skritch allegedly stayed for 5.
articles.social: A young dragon wants to extend its hoard into the cellar next door on Fish Street. The zoning board heard 41 neighbors over six hours, and the vote was 3 to 2. One of the no votes was cast by a man who had to leave to feed his cat. Would you sell your cellar to a dragon for 400 gold?
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell after sunrise, the Brindlemoor zoning board allegedly opened a zoning hearing on a young dragon's request for a dragon hoard annex in the cellar of the house next door on Fish Street. The dragon, a wyrmling named Ossira, says her pile of coin has outgrown the old tannery she lives in and that a hoard annex is, quote, 'a basic housing need.' The hearing lasted six hours, and I was there for five of them.

The neighbor, a retired net-mender named Pell Tarnowe, owns the cellar and does not want to sell. 'She offered me 400 gold,' said Tarnowe, who was holding a bucket of eels at the time. 'Then she offered me 400 gold and not eating me. I said the second part was not a fair thing to put in an offer.' Ossira's advocate, a lizardfolk clerk in a very clean collar, said the second offer was 'a friendly clarification.'

Forty-one residents spoke. Most were against the annex. A baker named Hobb Quillery worried about property values, noting that a dragon's hoard 'does things to the smell of a block.' A cooper named Dessa Rorke supported it, saying a hoard means foot traffic from thieves, and thieves buy barrels. Nobody could tell her what the barrels were for. Allegedly that was the point.
