Board chair Marlo Pennick asked whether the annex would raise the street's fire risk. Ossira's advocate said the cellar was already fire-rated, 'for a human fire.' Pennick asked what that meant. The advocate said he would need to check with the dragon, who was, at that moment, napping on the public benches. The board took a ten-minute recess. The recess was allegedly two hours, and a ceremonial sword in the corner caught the light the whole time. I will not discuss the sword. It was a really good sword.

Anyway. The Constabulary was called once, when a pigeon landed on the dragon's head and the dragon looked at it in a way the pigeon did not enjoy. I want to be clear that I did not cheer. Allegedly. A Constable wrote it up as 'a private matter between two animals.'

The vote came at the eleventh bell: three for, two against, with a condition that the annex be limited to 800 square feet and that the dragon not 'sleep on the property line.' Chair Pennick said the decision was final. One of the two no votes, councillor Wick Averell, missed the closing remarks because he had to go home and feed his cat. He told me the cat has been 'very unsettled' since the dragon moved in.

Tarnowe has until the next full moon to appeal. He says he will, and that he has hired the cleanest-collared lizardfolk he could find. The Lower City will be watching. I will be there too, near the sword.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Cellar Next Door
hook.text: A young dragon has won a permit to extend her hoard into a retired net-mender's cellar, and he has a week to appeal. He hires the party to find a defect in her paperwork, or a better cellar, before she takes possession.

npc.name: Pell Tarnowe
npc.want: To keep his cellar and his eels without being eaten.
npc.secret: The cellar has a bricked-up passage that leads somewhere he has never dared open.

location.name: Tarnowe's Cellar
location.text: A damp stone cellar full of eel barrels and old nets. The back wall sounds hollow, and the barrels tend to be warm.

campaign.rumor: They say the dragon doesn't want the cellar at all; she wants whatever is behind the back wall.

articles.title: Adventuring Party Spends 4,800 gp Reward on Ruined Keep
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party put its whole 4,800 gp quest reward into a ruined keep, then met the upkeep: 640 gp a month. Sterling Vanmoor sees equity.
articles.social: An adventuring party spent its entire 4,800 gp quest reward on a ruined keep outside Brindlemoor. The upkeep is 640 gp a month and the keep earns 90. The otyugh in the cellar pays the most rent. Would you have bought the keep, or the horses?
articles.content:
An adventuring party called the Iron Oath Company spent its entire 4,800 gp quest reward on a ruined keep outside Brindlemoor on Monday, and by Tuesday had learned what the keep costs to run. Staff wages, roof repairs, and the cellar tax come to 640 gp a month. The keep earns 90.

Let me be clear: this is the boldest pivot I have seen from a first-year party. Most adventurers take a reward and rent a room above a tavern, which is renting. The Iron Oath Company chose ownership. Ownership means a wall with your name on it, even when half the wall is on the ground.

The keep, Rookfall, came with twenty-two retainers. That includes a seneschal, nine kobold groundskeepers, and a cook who has not been paid since the previous owner. "We assumed they came with the deed," said the party's paladin, Odrick Harrow. "They did. That's the problem." The wage bill alone is 410 gp a month, and the seneschal has already requested a title.

Repairs are the part where the party's growth story gets interesting. The east tower leans. The drawbridge is a bridge in the sense that it is made of wood. A surveyor from Brindlemoor quoted 3,100 gp to make the roof stop being a skylight. The party's wizard, Pell Ansrow, proposed fixing it with a spell, then learned that the spell also costs money and that she had not been paid either.

Income is a different matter. Rookfall earns 90 gp a month, nearly all of it from an otyugh living in the cellar, which pays 60 gp in rent and has stopped answering questions about how it makes the money. The rest is a toll on a goat path. "We are exploring synergies," Harrow said. The party has since sold its horses, two of its swords, and one retainer's cousin.

I met a guildmaster once, in a carriage, and he told me that every asset is a liability until you stop looking at the ledger. I thought about it all night. The Iron Oath Company is not insolvent. It is pre-profit and pro-castle. When Brakka Stonesweat writes her gloomy column about this, remember she has never owned a drawbridge.

The party plans to rightsize the retainers from twenty-two to fourteen, a move the seneschal has called a mutiny. Harrow says he will personally fire the cook, then rehire her at half the pay, as a founder's gesture.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A keep is not a reward. It is a subscription with towers.
  • Read the retainer clause before you read the deed.
  • Keep one horse.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Keep That Ate the Reward
hook.text: A newly landed party of adventurers owns a crumbling keep, twenty-two unpaid retainers, and a monthly bill they cannot meet. They hire the PCs to find coin, clear the cellar, or find a buyer before the seneschal calls in the creditors.

npc.name: Odrick Harrow
npc.want: To make the keep pay for itself before the retainers quit.
npc.secret: He has already sold the east tower's stones to a quarry, and it is the tower that holds the roof up.

location.name: Rookfall Keep
location.text: A half-collapsed keep with a leaning east tower and a drawbridge that no longer lifts. Its cellar holds an otyugh that pays rent, which no one in the keep wants to explain.

campaign.rumor: They say the old owner didn't sell Rookfall, he fled it, and he's still owed wages by the cook.

articles.title: Green Hag's Detox Tea Turns 31 Folk Into Toads
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: A green hag's detox tea stall at the Brindlemoor market turned 31 customers into toads on Saturday. Brother Wendell prescribes broth, not cleanses.
articles.social: A green hag sold detox tea at the Brindlemoor market on Saturday, and 31 customers left as toads. The hag says that was the cleanse working as advertised. Brother Wendell says a pot of broth does the job for three coppers. Would you have drunk the tea?
articles.content:
Friends, a green hag running a detox tea stall at the Brindlemoor market turned 31 customers into toads on Saturday, and the infirmary has asked everyone to stop calling it a cleanse. The stall, marked with a hand-painted sign reading "Flush Your Humours," sold the tea at eight silver a cup. Every cup came with a free sprig of something green.

The first sign of trouble was a baker named Hilde, who sipped her cup, said she felt lighter, and then said "ribbit" in the middle of a sentence about rye. By noon the fountain square held thirty-one toads in good spirits and one very quiet bell ringer. Healers at the Brindlemoor infirmary cast remove curse in shifts, and as of this morning 27 are back in their own boots. Four are still toads. Their families report they seem rested.

The hag, who gave her name only as Mother Gristlewick, told reporters the tea was "traditional." She said the polymorph was a known side effect of any thorough detox and that her customers had been warned in the fine print, which was written on the underside of the cup. Several customers drank the cup before reading the underside.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9, which also called three owlbear cubs mere visitors, said the guild had no authority over market stalls but would "welcome a conversation about the toads." Reeve Maudrey Fennick has suspended the stall's permit and asked that the toads be kept off the road until Thursday.

Now the old herbals, friends. They say the body cleans itself: the liver, the kidneys, and the sweat on your brow do the work, and the old herbalists only ever asked you to drink water and go to bed. Healer Ansel Briar at the infirmary has tried every detox tea sold in Brindlemoor this year. He found not one that removes anything your body was not already removing, and a fair number of them contain laxatives, which is the same trick with a nicer sign. Nobody has yet tested a tea for toad content, but I would not be surprised.

I would like to say a word for the toads, who did nothing wrong. One was found sitting on the hag's own counter, looking at the tea with regret. Please be gentle with them. They have had a difficult weekend and several have already been stepped on by well-meaning cousins.

If you feel the need to cleanse, friends, sleep eight hours and drink a bowl of clear chicken-and-ginger broth. It costs three coppers, it turns no one into anything, and it has never once asked you to read the underside of a cup. My friend Nyx tells me there is a tea app that tracks your humours. Go outside, Nyx.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Underside of the Cup
hook.text: Four market-goers are still toads, and the hag who sold them tea has vanished from her cell. Their families will pay the party to find her and the antidote before the toads are sold as pets.

npc.name: Hilde Brannock
npc.want: To find whoever sold her the tea and get an apology in writing.
npc.secret: She remembers everything from the pond and knows where the hag keeps her cauldron.

location.name: The Flush Your Humours Stall
location.text: A canvas market stall with a cauldron that is always warm. The fine print on the cups is in Sylvan, and the cauldron is a little larger on the inside.

campaign.rumor: They say the four toads left are not the customers at all, and the hag swapped in real toads to save on antidote.

articles.title: Gelatinous Cube Storage Rents at 2 gp, Eats 11 Crates
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: A Brindlemoor landlord rents storage space inside a gelatinous cube for 2 gp a month, a fifth of warehouse rent. Eleven crates later, Barnaby has sums.
articles.social: A Brindlemoor landlord rents storage inside a gelatinous cube for 2 gp a month, against 9 gp for a warehouse. Forty-eight tenants signed up. Eleven crates have since dissolved, and the landlord calls it shrinkage. Would you store your boots in the cube?
articles.content:
A Brindlemoor landlord is renting storage space inside a gelatinous cube for 2 gp a month, while an ordinary warehouse bay on Tanner's Row costs 9 gp. Forty-eight tenants signed up in the first week. By Tuesday, eleven of their wooden crates had dissolved, and the rents have not changed.

Let me put this in loaves. (I have checked this four times.) At 3 sp a loaf on the current Loaf Index, a warehouse bay is 30 loaves a month and a cube bay is just under 7. That is a saving of 23 loaves per tenant, or 1,104 loaves across all forty-eight. It is the cheapest square footage in the barony, and every economist I know would call it a bargain right up to the moment the footage is digesting your furniture.

The landlord, a Mr. Orrin Pettibone of Pettibone Holdings, says the cube is "a premium preserving environment." Items suspended inside it do not rot, he explained, and thieves cannot reach them. He admitted that wood, leather and cheese are "subject to gradual repositioning," meaning the cube eats them. Metal, bone and anything made of gold pieces come through fine. Mr. Pettibone does not offer refunds, but he does offer what his lease calls "a complimentary re-shelving."

The tenants' claims are mounting. Dilys Wren, a candle-maker, lost four crates of tallow and says she can now see her own wax floating in the shape of a small duck. A cobbler named Harbin Vole lost every boot he owned that was not on his feet. Together the eleven lost crates are valued at 330 gp, or 1,100 loaves. That is more than the 96 gp the cube earns in a month, and it means the landlord is losing money in a way he has not noticed. It also means the 2 gp rent was never a price. It was a deposit on a loss.

This is the oldest mistake in real estate, and Sterling Vanmoor will no doubt say the cube is "disrupting storage." He will say the market will sort it out. I have read the lease and the market will not, because the cube does not read.

The Brindlemoor Watch has asked Mr. Pettibone to post a notice on the cube. He has done so, on a plank of wood, which the cube ate on Wednesday. A hearing is set for next week, to which tenants have been asked to bring only metal evidence.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, has been very quiet on the subject. I asked whether the boot was safe. She said it was, because she has moved it to a place "no one with a lease can find." I did not ask further. What this means for your pantry: do not store your flour in anything transparent that moves.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Cube Lease Audit
hook.text: A landlord has leased crate space inside a gelatinous cube and tenants are losing goods. A frightened cobbler hires the party to retrieve a locked strongbox before the cube digests its wooden lining, with a hearing in two days.

npc.name: Harbin Vole
npc.want: To recover his tools and his dignity before the hearing.
npc.secret: He stored a stolen ledger in the cube hoping it would dissolve.

location.name: Tanner's Row Cube Bay
location.text: A rented alley where a tame gelatinous cube sits in a cage of iron bars. Items drift inside it in slow orbit, and one boot has been circling for three days.

campaign.rumor: They say the landlord feeds the cube extra candles so it will spit out the good stuff first.

articles.title: Loot Split: Torchbearer's 'Equal Share' Is 20 of 3,000 Gold
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party promised its torchbearer an equal share of a 3,000 gold hoard, then paid itself first. The equal share came to 20 gold.
articles.social: A gnome torchbearer was promised an equal share of a 3,000 gold hoard. The party paid itself 500 gold each in advances first, so the equal share was 20 gold. He counted it three times and it really was equal. Would you have signed that contract?
articles.content:
Read the contract before the dungeon. Pim Dunnock, a gnome hired as torchbearer by an adventuring party called the Brass Pennant Company, got his promised equal share of a 3,000 gold hoard in Brindlemoor on Tuesday. The loot split gave him 20 gold. The five adventurers who hired him each took 520.

Here is how that works. The party's treasurer, a paladin named Tobias Venn, announced the loot split would be 'equal, as promised.' Before the counting, he took out 'advances': 500 gold for each of the five party members, 2,500 in all. Another 380 went to 'expenses,' which included rations, a wizard's hat, and a resurrection fund nobody has needed. That left 120 gold. Six people. Twenty each.

Everyone got the same. That is the trick. Nobody can say it wasn't equal.

'I counted it three times,' said Dunnock. 'It is equal. That's the worst part. I was hoping for a mistake I could be angry at.' He carried two spare torches, a rope, and the wizard's hat for nine hours underground. He lit the way past a falling-block corridor and a room full of green slime. His 20 gold was paid in copper, in a sock.

Ansel Pottage, steward of hirelings, read the contract aloud outside Chapter 9 on Wednesday, all the way to the end, which is more than the Pennants did. 'Clause four,' he said. 'Hirelings receive an equal share of the hoard.' He turned the page. 'Clause eleven. Advances are not part of the hoard.' Clause eleven, Pottage noted, is written in much smaller handwriting. A crowd of about thirty hirelings with their own torches booed the handwriting.

'I've lit tunnels for eleven years,' said Hesper Quillby, a torchbearer who came to watch. 'Every party says equal. I ask one question now: equal of what? Nobody has ever liked the question.'

Venn defended the split. 'The advances cover the risk we took,' he said. Dunnock replied that he held the light, so he was the one who could see the risk coming. Venn did not answer. He was counting something.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the advances 'pre-hoard liquidity' and said the guild is 'confident in the equality of the outcome.' That means they paid themselves first and then divided the crumbs fairly. A hearing has been set. Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor, who has seen a loot split go sour this week already, is said to be bringing her ladle.

The plain arithmetic goes like this. The usual hireling rate in the Undermaw is a half share. Split the 3,000 gold properly, and that comes to roughly 273 for Dunnock. He got 20. The Pennants have offered him a free ballad and a second 20 gold if he signs a scroll saying the first 20 was generous. He has asked to read the scroll to the end.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: Equal Of What?
hook.text: A hired torchbearer shows the party a contract promising 'an equal share' and a sock holding 20 gold. The hireling's steward wants the party's help finding the party that skipped town, and the gold they owe.

npc.name: Marta Tilbrook
npc.want: To make every hireling contract list the share in coin, in large print.
npc.secret: She wrote clause eleven for a party years ago and has regretted it ever since.

location.name: The Tally and Tallow
location.text: A cramped tavern where parties split their loot at a long table with a brass scale. Hirelings drink in the back, where the table is shorter.

campaign.rumor: Somebody said the Brass Pennants hid the real count of the hoard in a hat, and that the hat has since gone missing.

articles.title: Adventuring Party's Shortcut Turns 2-Hour Road Into 9
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party took a shortcut across the Brackwater border. A two-hour road became nine hours, one owlbear, and a diplomatic incident.
articles.social: An adventuring party skipped the bridge to save time. The shortcut took nine hours instead of two and ended in a border incident. Declaring their bag of holding took three hours, and it held a goat. Would you have trusted the ranger who said he knew a shortcut?
articles.content:
An adventuring party called the Mossy Pauldron Company took a shortcut across the Brackwater border on Fifthday. The road to the Ashenfold tavern normally takes two hours. It took them nine, and it ended in a diplomatic incident.

The plan was the ranger's. Dorrin Ashgrove, ranger, said he "knew a ford." The party skipped the three-copper toll at Quillmarch Bridge and waded the river upstream. Hour one: they were wet. Hour two: they were in Brackwater, unannounced, with swords.

Hour three belonged to an owlbear. It was in a meadow the ranger described as "empty last spring." The party went around it. The detour added two hours and a mile of bramble. Nobody was hurt. The cleric's dignity has been listed as missing.

Brackwater guards found them in hour five. Procedure was followed with great care. The party's bag of holding was declared at the border, as required. Its contents took three hours to list. Guard Captain Orwin Thatch reported that the bag contained forty-one torches, a goat, and "what appeared to be a second, smaller border." He asked that the second border be declared separately. The wizard said it was a map. The captain said maps are borders with fewer manners.

By hour eight, Envoy Teodra Hallowmere arrived to tax the matter. She taxes intent rather than goods, and she ruled the party's intent was "to save two hours at the realm's expense." The fee was set at two hours. Payable in time. The party owed nine, so they paid seven more standing in a corridor.

Ashenfold's side called it a provocation. Brackwater's side called it a Fifthday. Handshake between the two guard captains at the crossing: firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected, though one was later found in the goat. Tension rises to two siege-days, mostly from the owlbear.

"I said I knew a ford," Ashgrove told this correspondent. "I did not say it was a good ford. The ford is a ford." Asked whether he would take the bridge next time, he said the bridge costs three copper. Asked what the day cost, he stopped talking.

The company reached the Ashenfold tavern at the ninth hour. The tavern had closed its kitchen in the sixth. They ate field rations on the doorstep. This correspondent approves of the rations and of nothing else in this report.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Ford That Wasn't
hook.text: A merchant hires the party to escort a wagon on a "two-hour" shortcut between two quarreling baronies. The route crosses a border no one has mapped, an owlbear meadow, and a customs post that taxes intent.

npc.name: Orwin Thatch
npc.want: To finish one inspection without the goat being involved.
npc.secret: He has been quietly taking the shortcut himself and charging nobody for it.

location.name: The Upper Ford
location.text: A shallow river crossing that appears on no map and is knee-deep only on days the owlbear is elsewhere. A bramble bypass has worn a muddy road around the meadow.

campaign.rumor: They say the Upper Ford is only two hours long if you do not look back at the meadow.

articles.title: Long Rest Interrupted Four Times Over Watch Rotation
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: The Fourth Attempt's long rest on Level 5 was broken four times in one night, after the adventuring party could not agree who had the second watch.
articles.social: The Fourth Attempt tried to take a long rest on Level 5 and got four interruptions, zero hours of full sleep, and a fight over the watch rotation. The bard's ballad was counted as a shift. The wizard woke at 3 hit points. Would you take first watch, or would you also fake being asleep?
articles.content:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 5, A DEAD-END ROOM WITH ONE DOOR — The Fourth Attempt set out to take a long rest here on Tuesday night and got a long argument instead, followed by four interruptions, each of which reset the rest to zero. By dawn the adventuring party had slept, by my count, about nine minutes in total.

The trouble started before anyone lay down. The party's ranger, whose map was upside down on Saturday and who therefore holds no authority on anything, proposed four watches of two hours. The fighter asked for first watch, 'so I can sleep through the rest of it.' The wizard said casters need an unbroken block and asked for no watch at all. The cleric offered to take the last shift if somebody woke her. Nobody asked who would wake her. The party's bard, who asked to be named, volunteered to take 'the artistic watch,' meaning he would sit up and play something soft. Everyone agreed to this because they were tired.

Interruption one came at the first hour. Giant rats, nine of them, came through the door in single file, which I admit was polite. The fighter, on first watch, had fallen asleep standing up. The ranger woke, struck the first rat, and was told by the fighter that he was in the wrong order. Hour of fighting. Rest reset. Fighter 21 hit points (of 38), ranger 18 (of 29), one rat unaccounted for.

Interruption two was a stirge. One. It chose the wizard. The wizard woke at 3 hit points (of 22) and the cleric, who had been told she would be woken, was not, because the bard's watch was the one in progress and the bard had not finished his song. 'I thought the song was the watch,' he told me. 'A watch is a song with a purpose.' It was a short song. The stirge was gone by the second verse and so was the wizard's temper.

Interruption three was a wandering skeleton patrol. Interruption four was the same skeleton patrol, coming back, having forgotten something. I rolled poorly on this one and counted five skeletons both times. They had counted four. We have all been wrong in this room.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, had sat out the whole night in the doorway with a lantern and a copy of the contract. The two hirelings were under no obligation to keep watch, he said, as the contract assigns them 'carrying, holding, and the occasional heavy sigh.' He then read the watch clause aloud. There is no watch clause. 'That,' he said, 'is the clause.' I lost my seventh ten-foot pole of the season prodding that doorway for his sake.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the guild 'has no official position on rest,' and that the room has been marked 'Safe, mostly' on the map. The map is being reissued. The fighter, last seen napping on the stairs, says he will take first watch next time. Nobody believes him.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: The Watch Nobody Kept
hook.text: A party camped in a dead-end room has been attacked four times in one night, because every watch shift was either unmanned or doubled. A local guild wants a cleaner rotation drawn up, and the room's door may be less safe than the map says.

npc.name: Odrin Tallowmere
npc.want: He wants parties to hire him to write their watch rotation before they sleep.
npc.secret: He once slept through his own watch, and a skeleton patrol is how he lost his job.

location.name: The Dead-End Room
location.text: A single-door stone room on a dungeon level, marked safe on the guild map. Three corridors feed it, and one of them is never the same twice.

campaign.rumor: They say a skeleton patrol keeps coming back to that room because someone left a lantern behind, and it is not the party's.

articles.title: Bag of Holding 'Unlimited' Plan: 12 gp Buys 500 Pounds
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: Voidpocket Labs launched a 12 gp a month bag of holding plan with 'unlimited' storage. The limit is 500 pounds. Nyx tested it. Four eyes.
articles.social: Voidpocket Labs sells 'unlimited' bag of holding storage for 12 gp a month. Nyx packed their entire workshop in and found the limit is 500 pounds, plus a fee for taking things back out. Byte now speaks only in storage ads. Would you pay monthly to rent a pocket?
articles.content:
Okay. OKAY. Voidpocket Labs has launched the Endless Sack, a bag of holding subscription at 12 gp a month with, and I quote the box, "unlimited storage." I have been stuffing it for four days, and the actual limit is 500 pounds, which is exactly what a normal bag of holding holds. The word "unlimited" appears to be a feeling.

The setup is gorgeous! You tap the drawstring glyph, the sack hums, and the mana throughput is so smooth that my entire workshop went in without a ripple. Anvil, three workbenches, forty crates of firmware glyphs, a half-built clockwork heron. I was thrilled. Then the sack began to whisper, in a calm customer-service voice, "You have reached 91 percent of your unlimited storage."

I asked a Voidpocket representative, Odalys Brindlefoot, how a limit can exist in an unlimited plan. "The storage is unlimited," she said. "The sack is just very selective about what it counts as storage." She then explained that anything over 500 pounds is moved to the Overflow Dimension, where retrieval costs 3 sp per item and takes up to a fortnight. I have a portable hole in my coat that does this for free. I did not mention it, because I wanted to see the whole pricing page.

The runic latency on retrieval is, shall we say, a journey. I asked for a hammer and received a notification that my hammer was "being prepared." Forty minutes later the sack produced my hammer, a coupon for a second sack, and a spoon I have never owned. Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, looked into the opening and said, "Store more. Worry less. Terms apply." Then Byte climbed in and had to be fetched, at 3 sp.

There are flaws. The sack refuses to hold anything it considers "cloud-adjacent," which includes my rain cloak. It also sends a monthly report titled "Your Memories, Organized" listing everything I put in, including a sandwich I had forgotten. Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to touch grass and keep your belongings on your person. Brother Tumbleberry has never had forty crates of firmware glyphs and a heron. I also hate subscriptions, and I am paying it anyway.

Verdict: the idea is wonderful, the plan is a bag with a billing department, and I am keeping it. Four out of five beholder eyes.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below. Burns sustained: 0. Hammers retrieved: 1. Spoons acquired: 1. Eyebrows: fine, but the sack has offered to store them.

hook.title: The Overflow Dimension
hook.text: A merchant's Endless Sack has swallowed a guild's ledgers and the retrieval clerk says they are 'being prepared' for a fortnight. The party must enter the overflow pocket space to fetch the books before an audit.

npc.name: Odalys Brindlefoot
npc.want: To keep the subscription numbers up before the quarterly review.
npc.secret: She has been quietly moving unclaimed items to her own home.

location.name: The Overflow Warehouse
location.text: An extradimensional storeroom reached through any Endless Sack, lined with shelves labeled only by mood. Items drift to new shelves on their own.

campaign.rumor: They say the spoon in your pack was never yours, and the sack knows exactly whose it is.

articles.title: Wish Spell Makes Brindlemoor Vote Unanimous, 9-0, Forever
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A Burgess cast a wish spell so a drainage bill would pass unanimously. Brindlemoor's Council now votes aye on everything, adjournment included.
articles.social: A Brindlemoor Burgess cast a wish spell so a drainage bill would pass unanimously. It did, 9-0, and so did every motion after it, including a motion to adjourn and a motion to stay. The Council has now sat for 31 hours. Would you want a Council that always agrees with you?
articles.content:
Brindlemoor's Burgess Council voted 9-0 on Tuesday to pass a drainage bill, and has voted 9-0 on every motion since, after a Burgess cast a wish spell to guarantee the bill a unanimous result. The wish was granted as worded. The Council has now been in session for 31 hours, because the motion to adjourn also passed, and then so did the motion to remain.

The gentleman from Tanner's Row, Burgess Halvard Quill, admitted the casting to the Chamber after the third hour. He had wished, in his words, "that this bill shall pass unanimously," and the spell did not specify which bill. It has since passed unanimously a motion to rename the drainage bill, a motion to unrename it, and a motion declaring the Council's own motions void. The minutes record all three as carried. The clerk has stopped counting and begun listing.

Procedure matters here, so I will state it. A motion requires a mover, a seconder, and a vote. The spell supplies the vote. Burgesses who wish to speak against a motion rise, open their mouths, and say "aye." The lady from the Low Wharf, Burgess Odessa Marl, tried for forty minutes to say "nay" and produced a cough. She moved to censure Quill. It passed 9-0, with Quill voting aye on his own censure, which he says he did not enjoy.

The owlbear leash ordinance took nine hours and passed 5-4. This Council has passed forty-two items since Tuesday, including a levy on the gallery's seating, a proclamation that Thursday is canceled, and a resolution praising wish spells. By my count, Promises Made stands at thirteen. Promises Kept stands at the drainage bill, which has not yet drained anything.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said the town was aware of the situation. "We are aware of the vote," she told reporters, "and we are aware of the next vote, because it will be the same." She has asked a cleric to examine the Chamber. The cleric reported that the spell is not a curse, a charm, or an enchantment, but a contract, and that she does not read contracts for free.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the Council has never been so productive. "Nine to nothing, every time," the courtier said. "Nobody has ever wanted that more, or regretted it faster." Another motion arrived as the courtier spoke. It carried.

Quill has proposed a second wish to reverse the first, which requires a vote. The vote will be unanimous. The Council is divided, in spirit, on whether it should be.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Unanimous Chamber
hook.text: A town council has been bound by a wish spell to vote aye on every motion, and its members cannot say anything else. The magistrate will pay the party to find a way to lift the wording before the Council votes away something permanent, like the town's grain stores.

npc.name: Halvard Quill
npc.want: To undo the wish before anyone learns how much he has already voted away.
npc.secret: He cast the wish because he was bribed to guarantee a bill, and he still has the coin.

location.name: The Burgess Chamber
location.text: A round hall with nine carved chairs and a public gallery. Every door has been voted open and every window voted shut, and nobody can vote to reverse either.

campaign.rumor: They say the wish has a loophole: it only binds anyone who sits in a Burgess chair, so somebody just needs to sit in the wrong one.

articles.title: Adventuring Party Kicks Open Unlocked Bakery Door, Pays 9 gp
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party kicked in the door of a Fish Street bakery that was never locked and was billed 9 gold for the door and the loaves. Allegedly.
articles.social: A party of four kicked in a Fish Street bakery door at dawn, and the door was never locked. The town billed them 9 gold, including 14 loaves. The baker says the sign said PULL. Would you pay the bill or argue it with the Constabulary?
articles.content:
At roughly the first bell after dawn, an adventuring party calling itself the Gilded Pickaxes allegedly kicked in the front door of Tumblewick's Bakery on Fish Street, a door that was, by every account, unlocked. The Constabulary has since billed the four of them 9 gold for the door, its hinges, and 14 loaves that fell off the rack in the excitement.

The party's dwarf fighter, who asked to be called Brunna, says she heard 'suspicious scratching' inside. 'Dungeons have doors,' she told me, 'and doors have things behind them.' The things behind this one were Odo Tumblewick, a halfling baker, and a tray of cinnamon knots. Odo was allegedly scratching the oven with a spatula.

'The sign said PULL,' said Odo, who was holding what remained of the door. 'In red. In two languages. My niece painted a loaf next to it.' He pointed at the loaf. It was a very nice loaf. There was also a really shiny brass hinge on the cobblestones that I did not pick up, and I want that noted.

The party's wizard, Peppin Voss, says she had a knock spell ready and offered to cast it, but Brunna was already in the air. 'You cannot un-kick a door,' said Voss. A bystander, Marta Quill, who was eating a hot knot at the time, said the whole thing took under a second and then there was a long silence. 'The rogue looked at the handle,' she said. 'The handle was just a handle.'

The Pickaxes argued that a closed door in a delve is a challenge, not a courtesy. The Constabulary replied that Fish Street is not a delve, has never been a delve, and has a bakery on it. The bill, which is itemized, lists 5 gold for the door, 2 gold for the hinges, 1 gold for the bread, and 1 gold for a 'disturbance of the morning.' The last gold is allegedly for the cinnamon knot that Brunna ate afterward as a gesture of apology.

The party paid on the spot after a short vote the rogue lost. The Pickaxes say they will file an appeal to Chapter 9 on the grounds that an unlocked door should have been marked 'unlocked.' The Constabulary says it was. Odo says the sign now says PULL in three languages, and he has hired a gargoyle to point.

This is not the first time. Earlier this week an adventuring party was billed after a fighter kicked an unlocked tavern door, and the Constabulary has begun calling the pattern 'door enthusiasm.' Allegedly there is a form for it.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Door That Was Open
hook.text: The party is billed 9 gold in a small town after kicking in a shop door that was never locked, and the town will not let them leave until they pay or work it off. The baker offers a deal: guard his stall for three mornings while a rival tries to put him out of business.

npc.name: Odo Tumblewick
npc.want: He wants the party to repair his door and stop treating every closed entrance as a threat.
npc.secret: He really was scratching at his oven because a pest has been eating his sourdough starter, and he is afraid to say what it is.

location.name: Tumblewick's Bakery
location.text: A narrow shop with a new door painted PULL in three languages and a sign beside it with a loaf drawn on. The ovens are warm at all hours and something small keeps moving behind the flour sacks.

campaign.rumor: They say the baker keeps a spare door in the cellar because kicking it open has become the town's favorite pastime.

articles.title: Banshee Call Center Wins Service Award; Teacups Do Not
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: Wailwell Support, a banshee call center in Brindlemoor, won a service award Tuesday. Sterling Vanmoor calls the shattered glass engagement.
articles.social: A call center staffed entirely by banshees just won a service award in Brindlemoor. Callers report 212 shattered teacups a day, and the company calls that a 97 percent resolution rate. Would you stay on hold for a banshee?
articles.content:
Wailwell Support, the banshee call center on Tallow Row in Brindlemoor, won the Merchants' Service Excellence award Tuesday for the third year running. The company employs 60 banshees and fields roughly 4,000 calls a day, and its customers report that an estimated 212 teacups, 40 windowpanes, and one chandelier fail daily during hold music.

Some people see a wall of broken crockery. I see a customer who is fully engaged. Wailwell has reinvented the support call by making it impossible to ignore, and that, friends, is how you disrupt a sleepy industry.

Managing Wailer Ottoline Brass accepted the award in a gown of mourning silk and a pair of wax earplugs the size of walnuts. "Our resolution rate is 97 percent," she said, "because after the first wail, customers stop asking follow-up questions. Many stop asking anything." She declined to say how many callers were still hard of hearing after the quarter. Her staff shouted that number from the back of the hall, which was not helpful.

Complaints are down 80 percent, a figure Wailwell credits to a recent pivot: dissatisfied customers are now offered a free callback, in which the banshee visits their home. At least 31 households have taken the offer. Nobody has taken it twice.

Brindlemoor's clerks are unhappy, naturally. A delegate from the Hearing-Impaired Clerks' Lodge demanded that Wailwell issue earplugs to its callers. I would remind the Lodge that unions are a headwind to scale. When I met Guildmaster Aldous Pennyfarthing at a charity gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, a silent customer is a lost customer." I think about that every day, usually while wearing earplugs.

Wailwell is now scouting a second site for 120 more banshees and has asked the council for a noise variance that would let its roof sing after dark. The council, which still has not recovered from the lich merger and its skeleton clerks, said only that it would take the request under advisement as soon as it could find a room with unbroken windows.

Investors loved it. Wailwell stock jumped 11 percent on the news, and a rival firm, Murmur & Co., announced it was exploring "a quieter product," which analysts call a mistake. Brakka Stonesweat wrote a column calling the award a crime against ears. Brakka would, though. Brakka has never in her life been on hold with anything but a rock.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • If the customer shatters, the product is working.
  • Always ask your banshee for a testimonial before the first wail.
  • Wax is a business expense. Write it off.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Quiet Callback
hook.text: A shopkeeper begs the party to deal with the support firm whose banshee 'callback' keeps visiting her home. The firm will not cancel the service without a signed form, and the form is in the building where the wailing is loudest.

npc.name: Ottoline Brass
npc.want: To keep the Service Excellence award and win a second site.
npc.secret: She is deaf in both ears and has been bluffing every conversation for years.

location.name: Wailwell Support, Tallow Row
location.text: A three-story call center with wax-lined walls and a lobby full of cracked teacups. Its hold music is a single, sustained, very patient scream.

campaign.rumor: They say the banshees only wail because nobody ever listens to the complaint first, and one of them just wants a refund of her own.

articles.title: Potion of Healing Was Vial 11: Party Drinks Whole Satchel
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: The Brass Kettle Company drank 11 unidentified potions to find the healing one. It was the last vial, and the temple has questions. Soup is advised.
articles.social: Four delvers drank all 11 unidentified potions in a satchel to find the one that heals. It was the last vial, and it went to the only member who wasn't hurt. The broken ankle is still broken, and the rogue is still a draft. Would you have started with the smallest vial or the one that smelled like thunder?
articles.content:
Friends, four members of the Brass Kettle Company walked into the Temple of the Harvest Mother in Brindlemoor on Tuesday after drinking eleven unidentified potions in a row, hoping one of them would be a potion of healing. One was. It was the eleventh, and by then the only member of the party who still needed healing was the one who had already had it.

The trouble began on Undermaw Level Three, where the dwarf fighter Dagna Stoneweld broke an ankle on a loose flagstone. The party's satchel held eleven unlabeled vials. Wizard Pim Orchardsby proposed testing them one at a time, and the party agreed to a fair rotation, so that nobody went without a taste. "We didn't want anyone to feel left out of the hurting," Pim told the temple clerk, who wrote it down.

The results, as read from the intake ledger: one potion of diminution, which shrank the ranger to the size of a housecat and left her armor behind in a heap. One potion of climbing, which stuck the bard to the ceiling of the chamber for nine hours. One potion of gaseous form, which took the rogue up the corridor on a draught and has yet to bring him all the way back. Pim could no longer be seen from the left. The tenth vial was plain pond water with a grudge.

Then the eleventh vial, a potion of healing, was drunk by the bard, who was still on the ceiling and unhurt in every particular. He is reported to be in excellent health. Dagna's ankle was no better, and she carried the whole party to the temple on a hireling's cart, which Ansel Pottage of the Fourth Attempt offered to fetch for free, since his own party tried the same trick.

The old herbals say never to taste what you cannot name, and a recent temple study agrees, finding that the most common injury from a mystery tonic is the tonic. This is the second party this week to treat a satchel of unlabeled vials as a buffet. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the guild "has no rule against it, and is reviewing whether that is the problem."

The temple says the party's bill comes to 340 gold, which is less than one vial of healing at the shop on Tanner's Row, and I find that rather rude of the shop. Tip for any delver reading: a potion of healing is red, tastes faintly of honey, and is marked with a cross at the shop. Ask the person who sold it to you. Or pay a cleric three silver to look at it first.

Friends, if you must test your vials, test them on the least necessary party member, and have the wounded one go first. I'd pair this with a thick split-pea soup, and Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there's a scrying charm for naming potions. Go outside, Nyx.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Eleventh Vial
hook.text: A hungover party pays the PCs to retrace their trail up an Undermaw corridor and collect a satchel's worth of leftover vials before a rival crew drinks them. One vial is still unaccounted for, and it might be the real potion of healing.

npc.name: Pim Orchardsby
npc.want: To find the vial that undoes being invisible on one side before the temple bill comes due.
npc.secret: Pim relabeled two of the vials in a joke and cannot remember which.

location.name: The Temple of the Harvest Mother
location.text: A Brindlemoor temple with a long intake ledger, a soup kettle in the nave, and a bell clerks ring at anyone who tries to pay in unlabeled potions.

campaign.rumor: They say the pond-water vial wasn't pond water at all, just a potion of invisibility that got shy.

articles.title: Sixth Party Buys Same 'One-of-a-Kind' Treasure Map
articles.author: Barnaby Tallowmere
articles.excerpt: The Merry Kettles paid 40 gp for a one-of-a-kind treasure map, the sixth adventuring party to buy it this week. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
articles.social: Six adventuring parties each paid 40 gp for the same one-of-a-kind treasure map this week. The Merry Kettles found the other five camped around the X, and the seller has left town with 240 gp. Would you have bought the map, or asked to see the other copies?
articles.content:
The Merry Kettles, a four-member adventuring party from Brindlemoor, paid 40 gp on Monday for a "one-of-a-kind" treasure map sold by a stranger at a tavern table. By Thursday they had learned they were the sixth party to buy it that week. The stranger, who gave his name as "Honest Dabbs," has taken 240 gp in total and left on a cart.

The map shows a cellar on the third level of the Undermaw with a large red X and the words "DO NOT TELL ANYONE." The Merry Kettles reached the X on Wednesday and found five other parties already camped around it, sharing a kettle and comparing maps. The maps matched down to the coffee ring. (I have checked this against all six. Four times.)

The economics are plain, and I find them upsetting. At the current Loaf Index, 40 gp is 133 loaves, which is a family's bread for most of a season. Six buyers means Dabbs collected 800 loaves for one afternoon of ink, and he did it without a shop, a guild license, or a single honest measure of flour. A true one-of-a-kind item, like a good sourdough starter, is worth what it costs to make. A copy sold as one-of-a-kind is worth the copy price, which is about a copper and the price of ink.

"We should have known when he said 'exclusive,' and then said it again," said Hob Thornwick, the Kettles' halfling rogue. "He also had a stack of them under his hat."

The parties have done the sensible thing and formed a partnership. They have agreed to split whatever is under the X six ways, to dig in shifts, and to share the kettle. The treasure, once found, turned out to be one chest, which holds 62 gp and a note reading "SEVENTH PARTY ARRIVES FRIDAY." That is about 10 gp each, or 34 loaves, against the 133 each paid. Nobody has done that subtraction aloud. I did it twice and had to lie down.

Chapter 9 of the Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild says its own maps are accurate and sold at a fixed price, and it reminds adventurers that it sells them. Reeve Fennick has asked the town to "stop buying things from men called Honest." Dabbs was last seen heading toward Waterdeep with, by my count, six empty ink bottles and one very full purse.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, was told the story over tea. "A boot has never once sold me a map," she said. She is right, and I have underlined it.

What this means for your pantry: if a seller says a thing is one of a kind, ask for the receipt of the other five, and keep your 40 gp for flour.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

hook.title: The Seventh Copy
hook.text: A mapseller has sold the same "secret" map to every party in the region, and six rival crews are camped at the X. The party's patron wants the forger found before a seventh party arrives and the camp turns to a brawl.

npc.name: Dabbert Quillfeather
npc.want: To sell one more copy to a rich party before he reaches the next town.
npc.secret: He draws the maps from a real one he stole, and the real treasure is still somewhere he never marked.

location.name: The Crowded X
location.text: A third-level cellar with a red X chalked on the floor, crowded with six camps, three kettles, and a single trapdoor under the chalk. The floor sounds hollow in exactly one corner nobody has dug.

campaign.rumor: They say Honest Dabbs sold a seventh map to a gnome who paid in coin that turned to bread by dawn.

articles.title: Otyugh in the Sewer: 12 Night-Soil Haulers Strike
articles.author: Brakka Stonesweat
articles.excerpt: Twelve night-soil haulers in Brindlemoor stopped work Thursday after an otyugh moved into the Tanner's Row sewer. They want hazard pay and a longer pole.
articles.social: Twelve night-soil haulers in Brindlemoor walked off the job after an otyugh moved into the Tanner's Row sewer. They want hazard pay and a pole longer than 10 feet. The Reeve says the otyugh is 'a resident, not a hazard.' Whose side are you on?
articles.content:
Twelve night-soil haulers quit the Tanner's Row sewer Thursday morning. An otyugh moved in last week.

The haulers have worked the route for years. Now the route has a tenant with three tentacles, a mouth the size of a washtub, and what the haulers call 'a very firm opinion about who gets the buckets.' They want hazard pay, a ten-foot pole upgrade to a fifteen-foot one, and a lunch break that does not happen in the tunnel.

'I've hauled night-soil for twenty-two years,' said Durga Flintpocket, a cart-wheel greaser who joined the picket in solidarity. 'It used to be the worst job in Brindlemoor. Now it's the worst job with teeth.'

The otyugh, a creature that eats refuse and shares a lot of opinions with it, arrived through a collapsed drain from the Undermaw. Chapter 9 calls it 'a soft relocation.' That means it got out.

Haul foreman Tilda Brewfoot told this paper the monster is not even the main problem. 'It's polite enough. It takes what we give it. The trouble is we give it everything, and then it wants to talk about it.' She said the haulers have been asked to fill buckets with one hand and 'engage constructively' with the otyugh with the other. 'That means chat. For free.'

The town's offer so far is a new apron. Brakka has seen the apron. It is a regular apron. The haulers say it does not cover the front, the sides, or the tentacle-facing end.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick, reached outside the Reeve's Hall, said 'We are aware of the otyugh.' She called it a resident of Brindlemoor and asked the haulers 'to remember they have a duty to their neighbors.' Then she asked, quietly, whether anyone knew a bard who could sing to it.

The Sewer Board, a body of three men in good cloaks, issued a notice calling the strike 'a temporary reallocation of labor to the surface.' That means the haulers are standing in the street and the sewer is filling up. By noon the smell had reached the next ward. By two, a milkmaid on Cobbler's Lane was seen carrying her bucket in a sealed jar.

The haulers have not asked for much. Eleven silver more per night, a pole, and a rule that nobody is eaten before lunch. 'That last one's negotiable,' said Brewfoot. 'I'd settle for after lunch.'

A strike meeting is set for Friday at the Sleeping Mule. The tavern keeper has offered the cellar, which the haulers declined. They have been in enough cellars.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

hook.title: The Polite Thing Below
hook.text: Night-soil haulers refuse to enter the sewer because an otyugh has moved in, and the town is wading in filth. The haulers' foreman will pay the party to talk the creature out, or quietly move it, before the town turns on the strikers.

npc.name: Tilda Brewfoot
npc.want: Safe working conditions and fair pay for her crew without losing the contract.
npc.secret: She has been feeding the otyugh extra scraps for a week because it has started telling her useful gossip.

location.name: The Tanner's Row Sewer
location.text: A brick tunnel under the tanneries that smells worse than the tanneries. A collapsed drain at one end leads somewhere deeper and much older.

campaign.rumor: They say the otyugh has been counting the haulers by name, and that the one it doesn't mention is the one who's been skimming.

articles.title: Rogue Picks Envoy's Pocket, Starts Varnholt-Pellam Incident
articles.author: Grashka Ironjaw
articles.excerpt: A rogue in the Ember Ladle Company lifted a whistle from Pellam's envoy in Varnholt 'to see what he had.' Two realms now call it an act of war.
articles.social: A rogue from the Ember Ladle Company picked the pocket of a visiting envoy in Varnholt and got a brass whistle. It calms a ghost ship. Now the ship is loose, two realms are shouting, and the rogue says she was just curious. Would you have kept the whistle or handed it back?
articles.content:
A rogue from an adventuring party called the Ember Ladle Company picked the pocket of Envoy Dorrin Vask of the Pellam Isles on a Varnholt quay on Fifthday, "just to see what he had." What he had was a brass whistle, and the whistle kept the ghost ship Gannet's Regret quiet. The ship has been loud since noon. Pellam calls the theft an act of war. Varnholt calls it a customs matter and has billed the rogue a berth fee.

The rogue is Wren Tanglewick, a halfling, 26 years old by her own count. She told this correspondent she bumps people for fun. "I thought it was a coin purse," she said. "It was warm. It hummed." She blew it twice before anyone explained.

The ghost ship, still at the center of the Varnholt-Pellam visa dispute, answered the whistle by turning its bow toward the fish market. Witnesses say the lanterns swung on their own. A herring seller named Odo lost a cart and, he says, his composure. I would not mock Odo. Aim at the leaders.

Harbormaster Ilsabet Corvane of Varnholt reached the quay at one bell. She inspected the whistle, the rogue, and the pocket in that order. "Possession of foreign sacred goods requires a form," she said. "Nobody has a form for this. I will make one." She has not yet made one. Tension at the quay stands at about six siege-days and rising with the tide.

Vask arrived in a worse mood than the ship. He demanded the whistle back and a public apology to the Isles. Varnholt's offer was the apology, minus the whistle, plus a receipt. Vask declined the receipt. The handshake with Corvane lasted one second. Cold. Hidden dagger not detected, but I checked twice, and the rogue was standing right there.

The Ember Ladle Company has hired a lawyer, a gnome, whose opening brief argues that the whistle was "left in a public pocket." The party's paladin, who did not know about the theft, has asked to be removed from the story. The party's wizard says she tried to cast detect magic on the pocket and got a headache. Their cleric offered to pay the fine in healing. Corvane said healing is taxed.

Pellam sailors have moved a sloop to the harbor mouth. Varnholt has moved a toll chain across it. The ghost ship is parked between them, humming. Both sides called the arrangement "a de-escalation." Neither side moved.

Tanglewick was released on a promise to give the whistle back. She says she will. She also says it may have gone into a boot, and the boot into a wagon, and the wagon toward Brindlemoor. Corvane has set a deadline of Seventhday. After that the fee doubles. The ship, I am told, is not a patient creature.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

hook.title: The Whistle in the Boot
hook.text: A halfling rogue lifted a brass whistle that keeps a ghost ship docile, and a harbor town and an island nation both want it by Seventhday. The party must find the right boot before the ship, or the fine, gets out of hand.

npc.name: Tamsin Reedwhistle
npc.want: To process the whistle's paperwork before her supervisor notices the form does not exist.
npc.secret: She has quietly sold three ship-calming charms to smugglers and fears the whistle's owner will recognize her work.

location.name: The Dripping Berth
location.text: A harbor tavern that bills a berth fee per stool. Its back room has a sign that says 'No Ghosts', which the ghosts ignore.

campaign.rumor: They say the whistle was never Pellam's at all, and the ship answers to whoever has the loudest lungs.

articles.title: Ten-Foot Poles Recalled After Coming Up One Inch Short
articles.author: Hollis Delvewright
articles.excerpt: Pettibone & Vail recalled 900 ten-foot pole units that measure nine feet eleven inches. A pressure plate on Level 3 has noticed the difference.
articles.social: Pettibone & Vail has recalled 900 ten-foot poles for measuring nine feet eleven inches. On Level 3 of the Undermaw, a pressure plate sat exactly ten feet from the door and noticed. The fighter is at 6 hit points. Would you trust a pole that is one inch short?
articles.content:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 3, 140 FEET DOWN — A batch of 900 ten-foot pole units has been recalled by Pettibone & Vail Outfitters after Chapter 9 found them to measure nine feet eleven inches. The missing inch matters in a dungeon crawl, and I can report that a pressure plate on this level agrees.

The Fourth Attempt went in Tuesday with the new poles, which came in a handsome cedar-scented rack marked 'Trailmaster Reach.' The plate sits exactly ten feet from the door. The party's fighter tapped the floor at full extension, found it clear, and stepped forward the one inch the pole had not covered. Darts followed. He is now at 6 hit points. His boots, I am told, are at full health and at the bottom of a pit.

'It had a look about it,' said the party's bard, who asked to be named. 'The pole, I mean. It looked short. We assumed it was perspective.'

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the recall 'a soft correction' and said the poles remain 'substantially ten feet in spirit.' He added that permit fees for delves relying on short poles will be refunded, 'less the handling inch.' Asked what the handling inch is, Oddingwick said it is on track.

Pettibone & Vail says the error crept in at the mill, where a journeyman had been trimming each pole to fit a shelf. 'We want to be transparent,' a spokeswoman said. 'The shelf was nine feet eleven inches.' Customers may return any pole for a full refund, or exchange it for a pole of 'equal or greater feeling.' The firm is also offering a free one-inch extension sleeve, sold separately.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the sales receipt aloud to the party in the pit. 'It says ten feet,' he said. 'It does not say ten feet of pole.' He is owed two wages and an apology for the dart incident, and has asked that the apology be measured.

Shieldwall Mutual says the claim will be reviewed on whether the fighter's inch was 'reasonably his own.' A hearing is set before Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor on Monday. She has been bitten by a mimic and is not expected to be moved by an inch.

For the record, my own count stands at eight ten-foot poles lost this season. Three were the recalled kind. I rolled poorly on checking the receipt and reasonably well on the fourth, which I have kept, and which is now my twelve-foot stick. The mule remains unhurt and says nothing.

— H.D., filing from below

hook.title: The Handling Inch
hook.text: A shipment of ten-foot poles from a local outfitter is an inch short, and every trapped plate in the dungeon is calibrated to ten feet exactly. The party is hired to measure the dungeon's plates before someone steps one inch too far.

npc.name: Odrin Fellwick
npc.want: To keep his job without admitting the shelf was his idea.
npc.secret: He cut the poles to fit a shelf he built himself, and has already trimmed the next batch.

location.name: The Cedar Mill on Tanner's Row
location.text: A pole mill that smells of cut cedar and apology. Every shelf in the shop is a different length, and none are labelled.

campaign.rumor: They say the new poles are short because the mill ran out of cedar, and that it sold the rest to a mimic as a door.

articles.title: Sending Spell's 25 Words Go to Hellos; Reply Says Thanks
articles.author: Nyx Spindlecoil
articles.excerpt: An adventuring party cast Sending to ask a sage one question, then spent all 25 words on pleasantries. The reply answered only the pleasantries.
articles.social: A party in the Hollowmere Tombs cast Sending to ask a sage how to open a trapped door. The caster used all 25 words on hellos, the weather, and a gift basket. The sage replied with thanks and a note that the message cut off. Have you ever wasted a Sending, and what did you say instead of the question?
articles.content:
OKAY. Sending is the best spell in my notebook and I have just watched a party waste it with style. The Copperkettle Company, an adventuring party stuck outside a sealed door in the Hollowmere Tombs, cast Sending to ask a sage one question. Sending gives you 25 words out and 25 words back, and their caster spent every one of them on hellos. I was standing right there with a snack.

Here is the whole message, as recited by the caster, a halfling named Pim Tallowby, who has asked me not to print his face: "Greetings, dear friend, hope this finds you well, how is the family, lovely weather, did you get the gift basket, also, quick question about the." That is exactly 25 words. The runic latency was flawless. The door was not mentioned.

The sage, a retired lore-keeper at Candlekeep, replied within the round. "Family well, weather fine, basket received, thank you! Which question about the what? Message cut off. Also you forgot to say who this is." That is 24 words, and I have to admit it is a very efficient reply. It answers every question that was actually asked.

The party took this badly. The company's rogue, Sable Dunmoor, said she had told Pim to lead with the question in the planning session, "which lasted forty minutes and covered nothing else." Pim said it would have been rude to ask a favor cold. Sable said the door was a pit trap with a door on it and that the sage was not the one who would fall in. They recast the next morning, and Pim, now rattled, opened with "Door?" The sage answered "Which door?" and that was another 25 words gone.

It gets worse for the Company. Sending can be cast only so often, and a long rest is the price of a retry. By my count, the party has now spent two days of rations on a message that amounts to "Hello, how are you." Their cleric, Odalys Reed, has proposed carving the question into the door's frame as a sign-off sheet. My familiar Byte, who now speaks only in ad copy, said, "Say more with less. Try Sending Premium today." There is no Sending Premium. I checked twice, and I am a little sad about it.

Brother Wendell Tumbleberry, if you are reading, this is what I mean by "waiting." It is also, I will say, a lesson about touching grass, since the sage mentioned the weather was lovely and the party had not looked outside in three days. Four out of five beholder eyes for Sending itself. The Copperkettle Company gets two, and a pen.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 0. Words wasted: 25, then 25 more. Questions answered: 0. Eyebrows: fine, because I did not cast anything.

hook.title: The Door With No Question
hook.text: A party stuck at a trapped tomb door has twice failed to get a clear answer from a distant sage. The sage will help, but only if the party can phrase the question in 25 words or fewer, and a rival group is already sneaking toward the same door.

npc.name: Ilsabet Fenwright
npc.want: To answer exactly one question per day and then be left alone with her tea.
npc.secret: She built the trapped door decades ago and is embarrassed that nobody has simply asked her about it.

location.name: The Hollowmere Tomb Door
location.text: A sealed stone door at the end of a tomb corridor, scratched with failed attempts at opening it. Behind it is a pit trap, and the pit has a faint smell of rosemary.

campaign.rumor: They say the sage replies faster if you open with 'Who,' and slower if you ask about her cat.

articles.title: Bard Bluffs Past Town Gate, Council Hires Him as Guard
articles.author: Ottoline Vex
articles.excerpt: A bard talked his adventuring party past Tollwick's gate guard, 7-2. The Town Council then appointed him the new gate guard, at 14 silver a week.
articles.social: A bard bluffed his adventuring party past Tollwick's gate. The Town Council voted 7-2 to make him the new gate guard at 14 silver a week. His party now has to delve without him. Would you take the post, or run for the hills?
articles.content:
A bard has talked his adventuring party past the gate of Tollwick, and the Town Council responded by appointing him the new gate guard. The vote was 7-2. Pip Marrowtune, bard of the Gilded Pennywhistles, took the oath Thursday at a salary of 14 silver a week, with a spear he says he "has never held with intent."

The facts, as entered in the minutes: the Pennywhistles arrived at the north gate on Wednesday carrying no papers, a mule, and what Sergeant Odo Brack called "an unlicensed amount of lute." Marrowtune told the sergeant that the party was an advance inspection team from the Silver Marches, that the inspection was confidential, and that Brack had just failed it. Brack, who had stood at that gate for nineteen years, apologized, saluted, and held the portcullis himself.

The sergeant then fetched his superiors to be commended. That was the error. Marrowtune explained to the Town Council, in the same tone, that the gate was understaffed, that the sergeant was overqualified, and that someone of his obvious bearing should be running it. The gentleman from the Cooper's Ward moved the appointment before Marrowtune had finished the sentence. The lady from the Tanners' Ward seconded it while he was still on the verb.

Debate lasted four minutes. The council's last debate, on a goat ordinance, lasted three days. By my count this brings the session's Promises Made to nine and Promises Kept to the one about shorter meetings, which holds only if you ignore the goats.

The Pennywhistles had come to Tollwick to enter a barrow on the eastern road. Their fighter, Marta Gloam, said the party learned of the appointment from a notice nailed to the gate. "We turned around to ask him something and he was wearing a tabard," she said. "He told us it was a conflict of interest to leave." The party now has a fighter, a cleric, and a wizard, and a lute with no one to play it.

Marrowtune has already issued three decrees. Entry is free for "anyone who looks like they have a good reason." The toll is waived for bards. The mule has been made a deputy. Brack, reassigned to the night shift, declined to comment, but was seen offering his old keys to travelers and asking if they could see his papers.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the council meant only to "avoid the argument." Two councilors voted no, citing the principle that one should not hire the man who just lied to the staff. Their motion to revisit the matter was tabled. Nobody remembers by whom.

— O.V., from the gallery

hook.title: The Gate That Believes
hook.text: A silver-tongued stranger has talked a town council into making him gate guard, and the town's real guard captain wants him exposed before the barrow cult he fronts for arrives. The party must prove the lie without getting charmed into a uniform themselves.

npc.name: Odo Brack
npc.want: To get his post back without admitting he saluted a liar.
npc.secret: He let the bard through on purpose, because he was tired and wanted the night shift.

location.name: The North Gate of Tollwick
location.text: A stone gatehouse with a portcullis nobody has lowered in nineteen years. A deputized mule is tied to the winch.

campaign.rumor: They say the new gate guard has never once asked anyone for papers, and the toll box is full anyway.

articles.title: Ankheg Opens Sinkhole Under Fish Street Cheese Stall
articles.author: Skritch Mudwhistle
articles.excerpt: An ankheg tunneled under a Fish Street cheese stall and dropped it into a 12-foot sinkhole. Skritch has the scoop, and allegedly some of the cheese.
articles.social: An ankheg burrowed under a Fish Street cheese stall and dropped the whole thing into a 12-foot sinkhole. Forty wheels of cheese went down, and Reeve Fennick says the town is aware. The stall's owner wants his cheese back, and the ankheg allegedly wants it more. Whose cheese is it now?
articles.content:
At roughly the second bell past dawn, an ankheg tunneled up beneath a cheese stall on Fish Street and dropped the whole stall into a sinkhole 12 feet across. Forty wheels of cheese went down with it, along with the stall's awning and, allegedly, a very surprised goat.

'I heard a pop, and then the stall was lower,' said Dunstan Pell, the cheesemonger, who was holding a wedge of aged cheddar at the time. 'I'm still holding it. That's the only wedge I've got left.' Pell says the ankheg surfaced once, looked at the hole, looked at him, and went back down with the good brie.

Reeve Fennick of Brindlemoor arrived at the third bell and stood at the edge of the hole for several minutes. 'We are aware of the ankheg,' she said. Asked whether the town would pay for the cheese, she said the town was aware of that too.

The Constabulary roped off the sinkhole with the same rope they used for the owlbear in the laundry cart, which is allegedly still on the owlbear. Constable Hobb Tarrant said the rope was 'mostly there.' Neighbors report the ankheg has been heard chewing below ground since dawn and that it appears to be a loyal customer.

Deputy Registrar Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the sinkhole 'a soft opening of Undermaw Level Eight' and said permits for the new level would be available by the end of the week. Chapter 9 later corrected this: it is a sinkhole, and it is Fish Street's.

Also there was a really nice brass cheese knife on the ground by the hole. Anyway. I did not take it. It is in evidence. Allegedly.

Shieldwall Mutual says cheese lost to a burrowing monster is covered only if the cheese was 'properly staked,' which Pell says is not a thing people do with cheese. A claims adjuster was seen at the hole by midmorning measuring it and sighing.

Meanwhile the ankheg has become a Fish Street attraction. By noon, a line of about 300 neighbors had gathered to look in, and a boy named Wick sold tickets for a copper each from a crate. Wick allegedly cleared 11 silver before the Constabulary asked about his permit. The permit was allegedly in the sinkhole.

The ankheg is expected to resurface when the cheese runs out. Pell says that is not soon enough. He has asked the Reeve for a ladder, a net, and a better rope, in that order.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

hook.title: The Cheese Beneath the Street
hook.text: An ankheg has dug a sinkhole under the market and dragged forty wheels of cheese into its tunnels. The cheesemonger will pay 50 gp to anyone who recovers his stock before the tunnel collapses further.

npc.name: Dunstan Pell
npc.want: To get his cheese, and his stall's good name, back from the hole.
npc.secret: Half the lost wheels were bought on credit from a smuggler, who wants them returned.

location.name: The Fish Street Sinkhole
location.text: A 12-foot hole in the middle of a market street, ringed with rope and curious neighbors. The tunnel at the bottom smells strongly of brie.

campaign.rumor: They say the ankheg only wanted the cheese, and that there's a second one under the dairy.

articles.title: Party Sells Unknown Ring for 5 gp; It's a Ring of Protection
articles.author: Sterling Vanmoor
articles.excerpt: A Brindlemoor party sold an unidentified ring for 5 gp because nobody cast Identify. By morning it was a ring of protection, priced at 4,000 gp.
articles.social: A party of four sold a plain-looking ring for 5 gp because nobody had prepared Identify. The next morning it sat in the shop window as a ring of protection for 4,000 gp. The shopkeeper says the customer set the price, and she now sells a 12 gp appraisal subscription. Would you have spent the 100 gp pearl to cast Identify?
articles.content:
The Lantern Hollow Four, a Brindlemoor adventuring party, sold an unidentified ring to a curio dealer for 5 gp on Tuesday because nobody had prepared the Identify spell. By Wednesday morning the same ring sat in the window of Marrow & Finch Curios as a ring of protection, tagged at 4,000 gp. Let me be the first to say it: this is the most inspiring story of the quarter.

Some people see a party robbed of 3,995 gp. I see a shopkeeper who invested in verification. Proprietor Odalys Marrow spent a single afternoon and one ten-minute ritual to turn a 5 gp trinket into a four-thousand-gold asset. That is an 800x return, and frankly the party should be sending her a thank-you scroll for the learning opportunity.

The party had the chance to disrupt itself. Wizard Tobin Aldermere says Identify costs 100 gp in pearl dust, plus a spell slot, plus a ten-minute rest nobody wanted to take in a corridor that smelled like wet owlbear. "We voted," he told me. "The vote was three to one, and the one was me, and I was right, and it has not helped." The cleric, Brother Tamsin, had a slot but had spent it earlier on Goodberry. He describes the decision as "a wholesome use of resources."

The ring did not go quietly into the 5 gp bin. According to the party's own account, it hummed whenever a goblin was nearby, and the rogue wore it for four rooms without noticing that every arrow she met was a little bit late. Sources close to the rogue confirm she thought the arrows were just being polite.

Marrow, for her part, refused to apologize. "The customer set the price," she said, leaning on a counter built entirely out of other people's unidentified wands. "They said five. I said sold. I did not say I would not look afterward." She also announced a new Appraisal Subscription, 12 gp a month, for adventurers who would like to learn what they own before they sell it. Early adopters get a free glass of cider, which is also unidentified.

I once met a retired guildmaster at a gala, and he told me, "Sterling, information asymmetry is just a gap in the market with a cover charge." I wrote that on a napkin and I still have it. Marrow has clearly read the napkin.

Shieldwall Mutual declined to comment on whether a party that sells its own armor class is covered. The Brindlemoor Public Cellars Board says shop windows are not its department. A rival columnist has already written six hundred words calling this "theft with a scroll case", which shows how little some people understand scale.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Identify every item before you sell it, or become the supplier.
  • A 5 gp ring is a 4,000 gp ring that hasn't met its audience yet.
  • When the wizard votes no, schedule a long rest.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

hook.title: The Ring in the Window
hook.text: The party sold a ring for pocket change and found it in a shop window priced at a king's ransom. The shopkeeper is within her rights, so the party must either buy it back, steal it, or find out why the ring was in a corridor nobody remembers visiting.

npc.name: Odalys Marrow
npc.want: To keep the shop's reputation as the only honest appraiser in town.
npc.secret: She casts Identify on everything she buys, and has learned the town's richest families once sold her their own stolen heirlooms.

location.name: Marrow and Finch Curios
location.text: A narrow shop with a bell that rings a half second after anyone leaves. Every item has two price tags, and one of them is crossed out in the wrong direction.

campaign.rumor: They say the ring was never lost in the first place, and that a certain guild clerk keeps dropping them in dungeon corridors on purpose.

articles.title: Basilisk Eye Exam Clinic Petrifies 24 Patients
articles.author: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
articles.excerpt: A free eye clinic in Brindlemoor turned 24 patients to stone on Wednesday after hiring a basilisk to hold the chart. Brother Wendell recommends carrots.
articles.social: A free eye clinic in Brindlemoor hired a basilisk to hold the chart, and 24 patients turned to stone before lunch. Reeve Fennick says the town is 'aware of the statues.' The chart was read perfectly, though. Would you let a basilisk hold your eye chart for a free exam?
articles.content:
Friends, a free eye-screening clinic on Lantern Street in Brindlemoor petrified 24 patients on Wednesday morning, after the clinic hired a basilisk to hold up the eye chart. The creature, a young one named Pebble by the staff, was taken on because it "works for crickets and never asks for a raise."

The clinic's director, Optician Dessa Wrenfield, told this paper the basilisk was meant to stay behind the screen. "Patients read the letters off the back of its crate," she said. "The crate had a slot. The slot was, in hindsight, a design choice." By the time the second row of seated patients had gone grey and stiff, the line outside was still reading the sign aloud, and several joined the waiting room in stone.

Chapter 9 spokesman Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said the incident was "a soft launch of a statuary service." Reeve Maudrey Fennick, who had her own appointment at eleven, was less cheerful. "We are aware of the statues," she said, standing a respectful distance from the door with her eyes on her boots. "We would like them to stop being aware of us."

The temple of the Harvest Mother sent a healer with greater restoration, and by dusk all 24 patients were soft and grumbling again. Each paid a copper for the privilege, which is the first time a Brindlemoor temple has been cheaper than a free clinic. Patient Hobb Lindenfoot, a cobbler, said the worst part was the draught. "I was a statue by the window. Pigeons have opinions."

Now the old herbals, as my grandmother's grandmother wrote them, hold that carrots, leafy greens, and plenty of rest keep the eyes bright, and a recent study agrees that folk who eat vegetables daily keep their sight longer. Neither says a word about basilisks, which I take to mean the herbalists thought it went without saying. If your eyes ache, friends, see a person with eyes of their own and a chart that does not breathe.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has declined all 24 claims, ruling petrification a "pre-existing hardness." Wrenfield has reopened the clinic on a smaller scale, with a mirror shield and a sign reading ALL VISITORS PLEASE WEAR BLINDFOLDS. Pebble has been reassigned to the cricket department. My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that tests your eyes now. Go outside, Nyx, and look at a tree.

Tonight, make a carrot-and-ginger soup. It is good for the eyes, and nobody has ever been turned to stone by a ladle.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

hook.title: The Chart Holder
hook.text: A free eye clinic in town has gone quiet, and two dozen stone figures stand in its waiting room. The clinic's director offers the party 50 gold to quietly get her basilisk out of the building, and she would rather the temple not hear of it.
